# Implement a Story

Story: the arguments from the invocation (empty → `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/next-story.ts`; a story
already `in-progress` is finished first). `--fast` and `--prototype[=ui|logic]` are flags, not the story ID: strip
them before resolving the story.

The main session writes the code; subagents only review, and only in the full domain lane. One checkpoint belongs to
the user: the **merge** (step 7). Everything before it runs without asking – a `ready` story is good enough to build
up to the pull request, and the acceptance tester accepts the story, not the user – unless the story turns out to be
wrong (see *When the story is wrong*), a seam is missing from the catalog (step 2), or the user asked for a prototype
(step 1b – the verdict is theirs).

## Two lanes

| Lane | Stories | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Domain** (default) | `type: domain` (legacy `story`) | TDD per Gherkin scenario, scenario ↔ test traceability, diff-scaled review, acceptance tester's verdict |
| **Fast** | `type: chore`, `type: task`, or `--fast` on such a story | branch → implement → lint/typecheck/unit tests → verify → PR; no Gherkin matching, no formal review pass, the user merges |

`--fast` on a `type: domain` story is ignored: the story has a command and scenarios, so it takes the domain lane.
If a "chore" turns out to touch a command, a migration or authorization, stop and say so – risk decides the lane,
not the label.

Engineering conventions: `docs/engineering/conventions.md` – read it if it exists; it describes the module layout,
how commands and read models are built, and the **seam catalog**.

Project profile: `.claude/project.json` – default branch, code roots, commands, preview provider, pull-request tool.
Read it instead of assuming `main`, `npm` or GitHub.

## 1. Prepare
1. Working tree clean, on the default branch (`repo.defaultBranch`), up to date (`git pull`). Otherwise stop and tell
   the user.
2. With a tracker (`backlog.provider` ≠ `local`), pull first (`/backlog-sync pull`) and check that the story has its
   `external` key – an unlinked story never reaches `ready`, so stop and report instead of implementing a stale mirror.
3. `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/story-context.ts ST-NNN` – the context pack: story, exact test titles,
   dependencies, events/commands/rules/invariants, glossary, data model, ADRs. Read it completely; it is your
   source, not memory.
4. `git switch -c st-NNN-<slug>` (slug from the file name), then
   `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/story-status.ts ST-NNN in-progress` and commit `ST-NNN: start`.
5. **Pick the lane** and say it in one line: fast lane for `chore`/`task`, domain lane otherwise. The fast lane is
   a shortcut for non-domain work, never a way to skip a risk review.

## 1b. Prototype (only when asked)

Only with `--prototype`, or when the user explicitly asks during the story. A `ui: true` story whose screen shape is
still open was not `ready`; this is the exception that settles it before the test plan. Load the `prototype` skill and
follow it.

1. **Standalone first.** Delegate to `ux-designer`: question, branch (`ui` or `logic`), variants/scenarios, timebox,
   target `docs/prototypes/<slug>/`. It writes the self-contained HTML file. The user decides.
2. **In-app only when the question needs the real page** – an existing route, real data, the real header and
   sidebar. You build the throwaway route or the `?variant=` gate yourself, following the project's routing
   convention; the `ux-designer` defines the question and variants and reviews the result. The prototype stays out of
   the production path and is captured on `prototype/<slug>`.
3. **Capture.** Commit `docs/prototypes/<slug>/` (or the in-app prototype) on `prototype/<slug>`, return to the story
   branch, and write the verdict into the story's `## Context`: `Prototype: prototype/<slug> – <question> – <verdict>`.
   A recurring rule goes to `ux-designer` for `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md`.
4. **Then decide.** If the prototype only settles layout and the scenarios still hold, continue with step 2. If it
   changes behaviour or a scenario, the story goes back to `review` (see *When the story is wrong*), the main session
   revises it, the spec linter runs and the user approves it again. The branch stays.

## 2. Test plan

**Domain lane.** Call the `skill` tool for `tdd` (and `codebase-design` when a new module or interface is involved).
Show one table and go on to step 3 without waiting:

| Scenario (exact test title) | Seam | Test type | Test file |
|---|---|---|---|

- One row per Gherkin scenario – at most 4 by the 1-command rule.
- Seams come from the seam catalog in the engineering conventions. A seam not in the catalog is a decision for the
  user – the one case where you stop here and ask.
- Name anything the story leaves open. Don't guess – see *When the story is wrong*.

Seams from the catalog are the "confirmed seams" the tdd skill requires; the user approved the catalog.

**Fast lane.** No scenario table. Name the files or packages you will touch and the unit/integration tests that
cover them; the story's checklist is the acceptance. If it already has scenarios, keep them as a sanity check but do
not create `ST-NNN:` test titles.

## 3. Red → green (domain) / implement (fast)

**Domain lane:**
- Per row: write the test (title exactly `ST-NNN: <scenario title>`), run it and see it fail for the right reason,
  write the minimal code to pass, run it green. Commit: `ST-NNN: <scenario title>`.
- Domain IDs in the code: commands, events, read models and policies carry their ID from `events.yaml`
  (`CMD-ReportProblem`, `EVT-ProblemReported`, …). New code uses the words of `CONTEXT.md`; a new term goes into
  `CONTEXT.md` first (domain-model skill).
- Never weaken or delete an existing test to get green. If a test from an earlier story blocks you, its story and
  this one contradict each other → *When the story is wrong*.

**Fast lane:**
- Implement the task, keep the change as small as the checklist says, and add or update unit tests where the change
  can break behaviour. No test-title matching, no scenario traceability.
- Tick each checklist item in the story file as it becomes true (`- [x] …`).
- If the work turns into domain behaviour (a new/changed command, event or invariant), stop: the story is the wrong
  type. Send it back to `review` as a `domain` story instead of deciding it in code.

**Both lanes** – hooks help on the way: formatting and lint after every write, the quick gate (type check + related
tests) before you finish a turn. In a monorepo, run the affected set for the packages you touched before the full
gate: `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/affected.ts --changed <files>` (or `--base <defaultBranch>`), then
execute the printed command. It follows shared-library dependents; `verify.ts` still runs everything at the end.

## 4. Verify
`node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/verify.ts` (with `--e2e` when browser tests exist) must be green: lint incl.
module boundaries, type check, tests, events and stories valid, scenario ↔ test and domain ID traceability. Language
warnings: fix or justify.

The full `--e2e` run happens **once, before the push**. During red → green run only the spec you are working on;
after the refactor (step 6) run `verify.ts` without `--e2e` plus the specs the refactor touched – CI runs every
browser test on the pull request anyway (check `e2e`).

## 5. Review (domain lane only, scaled to the diff)

**Fast lane: skip this step.** No `code-reviewer`, no `acceptance-tester`, no review file. The gate is step 4 plus
the user's merge. If the diff touches authorization, input handling, a migration or security headers, say so and offer
the normal review anyway – the lane follows the risk, not the label.

**Domain lane.** Push the branch (`git push -u origin st-NNN-<slug>`) so a preview deployment exists, when the project
has one (`review.preview` in `.claude/project.json`: `vercel`, `netlify`, … – use the provider's MCP or CLI, or the
pull request's preview comment). Otherwise there is no preview and the reviewers work from the code.

Pick the lane from the **diff**, not from a size label:

**Light lane** – all of these hold: the diff is texts, layout, styles, links or docs; no command or route added or
changed; no input handling (no request handler, form action); no migration; no new dependency.
- Only `acceptance-tester` – task: story ID, base ref, the preview URL (if known), and: *also check the diff briefly
  against the engineering conventions (texts from the catalogs, the shared page frames, domain language) and list
  deviations as minors.* Writes `docs/reviews/ST-NNN-acceptance.md`.
- No `code-reviewer`, no extra code or security pass.

**Normal lane** – everything else. Start in **one** message:
- `code-reviewer` – task: story ID, base ref, the context pack command. Writes `docs/reviews/ST-NNN-code-review.md`.
- `acceptance-tester` – task: story ID, base ref, the preview URL (if known). Writes `docs/reviews/ST-NNN-acceptance.md`.
- Only when the **diff** touches the command layer or other shared platform code: ask the `code-reviewer` for a
  second, bug-focused pass over the diff.
- Only when the **diff** touches input handling, login/roles/session, uploads or files, or security headers/CSP: ask
  the `code-reviewer` for a security-focused pass.

Both reviewers report findings and never create stories. A finding is **fixed in this story** or becomes an open
question to the developer (step 6) – there is no follow-up ticket.

Say which lane you picked and why in one line.

## 6. Refactor
- Fix all blockers and majors **inside this story**, and the minors you agree with; say which minors you skip and why.
  Where a finding offers options, apply the recommended one without asking; ask only when no option is recommended.
- **No follow-up stories from reviews.** A finding that is too large for this story is either:
  1. a **question to the developer** in the review file and in the wrap-up (with evidence and options), or
  2. a line in `## Out of Scope` / a row in `OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` when it is a real decision for the user.
  Only the main session and the user decide whether it becomes a new story; the reviewers never do.
- Refactor only with green tests; the tests must not change unless they were wrong (then say so). Run `affected.ts`
  for the touched packages, then `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/verify.ts` again (without `--e2e`) plus the
  browser specs the refactor touched – see step 4.

## 7. Done, acceptance and merge → user checkpoint

**Fast lane:** tick the last checklist item, then
`node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/story-status.ts ST-NNN done` (it refuses while a checklist item is open).
Commit `ST-NNN: done`, push, open the pull request.

**Domain lane:** the **acceptance tester's verdict is the acceptance**: the story is `done` in the pull request, so
the user only merges.
1. After the refactor, check the verdict in `docs/reviews/ST-NNN-acceptance.md`. `accepted` or `accepted with
   remarks` → continue. `not accepted` → fix the gaps in the story and run the `acceptance-tester` again, until it
   accepts. Only when something goes badly wrong – the verdict stays `not accepted` after a second round, a scenario
   can't be met as written, the preview shows a defect the tester couldn't see – ask the user, the way *When the story
   is wrong* describes.
2. `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/story-status.ts ST-NNN done` – refuses unless every scenario has its test
   (domain) or every checklist item is ticked (chore/task/tech task/spike) and all dependencies are done. Commit
   `ST-NNN: done`, push.
   - GitHub: the status change closes the linked issue.
   - Jira: `story-status.ts` prints the transition it could not make (MCP is agent-only). Run
     `jira_get_transitions` + `jira_transition_issue` on the printed key, then push the story body once
     (`/backlog-sync push`).

**Both lanes – the pull request:**
3. Title `ST-NNN: <story title>`, body = the scenarios as a checklist (domain) or the task checklist (fast lane),
   links to the story and the review files (if any), the acceptance verdict (domain), the preview URL, remaining
   minors/questions, and anything the user must approve (a conventions change). (No `gh` CLI, or it isn't
   authenticated: push and give the user the compare URL `git push` prints.)
4. **The user merges** – on the preview if they want to look first. Afterwards: back to the default branch and
   `git pull`.

## 8. Wrap-up
Summarize in a few lines: lane taken, scenarios implemented or task completed, review findings fixed/skipped, open
questions handed to the developer, glossary/ADR changes. Then:
- Suggest `/improve-codebase-architecture` after the foundation stories, when a bounded context is complete, or about
  every 8–10 done stories.
- Name the next story (`node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/next-story.ts`) and tell the user to start it in a fresh
  session (`/new`, then `/implement`): every turn re-reads the whole session, so a second story in the same one costs
  several times the first.

## Spikes
A spike answers its **Question** within its **Timebox** – no test plan, no TDD for throwaway experiments.
- A UX or state-model spike is a prototype: load the `prototype` skill, keep the question and timebox in the story,
  and capture the verdict the same way (step 1b).
- Before starting, tell the user the timebox and what will be kept (skeleton code that becomes the application gets
  tests and passes verify).
- Tick each checklist item in the story file as it is answered; write results where the item says (an ADR's
  consequences, `OPEN_QUESTIONS.md`). A new decision → ADR with `status: proposed` (architect skill); the user accepts.
- Timebox exhausted → stop, document what is known, and ask the user how to continue.
- Review: `code-reviewer` only for code that is kept; `acceptance-tester` checks the checklist evidence.

## When the story is wrong
Never guess. When a scenario contradicts another story, a rule or an ADR, can't be tested as written, or leaves a
decision open:
1. Stop implementing that part. Mark it `[OPEN]` in the story and add a row to `docs/stories/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md`.
2. `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/story-status.ts ST-NNN review` and tell the user. The fix goes through
   discovery in the main session: revise the story, run the spec linter, and let the user approve it again
   (`/review-stories`). Work already done on the branch stays.
3. New domain term → `CONTEXT.md` (domain-model skill). Architecture deviation → a `proposed` ADR (architect skill).
   An accepted ADR is never edited; the hooks block it.
4. A `done` story is never reopened – a change to finished behaviour is a new story.

## Foundation stories
The first stories build what all others rely on, so they also set up the workflow's tooling:
- A single quality command in the repository's task runner (e.g. `npm run verify`) that runs
  `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/verify.ts`. CI runs the same command.
- Scripts for `lint` (including module-boundary rules), `typecheck`, `test` and, when there are browser tests,
  `test:e2e`. Record them under `commands` in `.claude/project.json` – verify and the hooks read them there.
- The application's lint and type-check configs exclude `.claude/` and `docs/`; the tooling has its own tsconfig.
- The hooks use Prettier, ESLint, `tsc` and Vitest when they are installed in the app's `node_modules`. With a
  different toolchain, adapt `.claude/hooks/stop-gate.ts` and `code-check.ts` – they are plain Node.
- **After the foundation exists** write `docs/engineering/conventions.md` from what now exists (not before):
  module layout, how a command runs (transaction, journal, authorization, version check), a read model, a
  time-based rule, UI texts, test data builders and the fixed clock, and the **seam catalog** – which seam each
  kind of code is tested at. The user approves it; then re-check the stories that depend on the foundation's results.

# Improve Codebase Architecture

Surface architectural friction and propose **deepening opportunities**: refactors that turn shallow modules into deep ones. The aim is testability and AI-navigability.

This command is _informed_ by the project's domain model and built on a shared design vocabulary:

- Call the `skill` tool with `codebase-design` for the architecture vocabulary (**module**, **interface**, **depth**, **seam**, **adapter**, **leverage**, **locality**) and its principles (the deletion test, "the interface is the test surface", "one adapter = hypothetical seam, two = real"). Use these terms exactly in every suggestion, and don't drift into "component," "service," "API," or "boundary."
- The domain language in `CONTEXT.md` gives names to good seams; ADRs in `docs/adr/` record decisions this command should not re-litigate.

## Process

### 1. Explore

**Scope before you scan: YAGNI.** Deepening a module pays off by making future changes to it easier, so put extra weight on the parts of the codebase that have recently changed. Decide *where* to look before you look:

- If the user named a direction (a module, a subsystem, a pain point), take it, and skip the inference below.
- Otherwise, walk back a good stretch of the commit history (`git log --oneline`) to find the codebase's hot spots, the files and areas that keep coming up, and let those paths pull your attention first. If the changes are scattered with no clear hot spot, widen the net.

Read the project's domain glossary (`CONTEXT.md`) and any ADRs in the area you're touching first.

Then spawn a sub-agent to walk the codebase. Don't follow rigid heuristics; explore organically and note where you experience friction:

- Where does understanding one concept require bouncing between many small modules?
- Where are modules **shallow**, with an interface nearly as complex as the implementation?
- Where have pure functions been extracted just for testability, but the real bugs hide in how they're called (no **locality**)?
- Where do tightly-coupled modules leak across their seams?
- Which parts of the codebase are untested, or hard to test through their current interface?

Apply the **deletion test** to anything you suspect is shallow: would deleting it concentrate complexity, or just move it? A "yes, concentrates" is the signal you want.

### 2. Present candidates as an HTML report

Write a self-contained HTML file to the OS temp directory so nothing lands in the repo. Resolve the temp dir from `$TMPDIR`, falling back to `/tmp` (or `%TEMP%` on Windows), and write to `<tmpdir>/architecture-review-<timestamp>.html` so each run gets a fresh file. Open it for the user (`xdg-open <path>` on Linux – under WSL `wslview <path>` or `explorer.exe "$(wslpath -w <path>)"` –, `open <path>` on macOS, `start <path>` on Windows) and tell them the absolute path.

The report uses **Tailwind via CDN** for layout and styling, and **Mermaid via CDN** for diagrams where a graph/flow/sequence reliably communicates the structure. Mix Mermaid with hand-crafted CSS/SVG visuals: use Mermaid when relationships are graph-shaped (call graphs, dependencies, sequences), and hand-built divs/SVG when you want something more editorial (mass diagrams, cross-sections, collapse animations). Each candidate gets a **before/after visualisation**. Be visual.

For each candidate, render a card with:

- **Files**: which files/modules are involved
- **Problem**: why the current architecture is causing friction
- **Solution**: plain English description of what would change
- **Benefits**: explained in terms of locality and leverage, and how tests would improve
- **Before / After diagram**: side-by-side, custom-drawn, illustrating the shallowness and the deepening
- **Recommendation strength**: one of `Strong`, `Worth exploring`, `Speculative`, rendered as a badge

End the report with a **Top recommendation** section: which candidate you'd tackle first and why.

**Use CONTEXT.md vocabulary for the domain, and the `/codebase-design` vocabulary for the architecture.** If `CONTEXT.md` defines "Order," talk about "the Order intake module," not "the FooBarHandler," and not "the Order service."

**ADR conflicts**: if a candidate contradicts an existing ADR, only surface it when the friction is real enough to warrant revisiting the ADR. Mark it clearly in the card (e.g. a warning callout: _"contradicts ADR-0007, but worth reopening because…"_). Don't list every theoretical refactor an ADR forbids.

See [HTML-REPORT.md](HTML-REPORT.md) for the full HTML scaffold, diagram patterns, and styling guidance.

Do NOT propose interfaces yet. After the file is written, ask the user: "Which of these would you like to explore?"

### 3. Grilling loop

Once the user picks a candidate, call the `skill` tool with `grilling` to walk the decision tree with them: constraints, dependencies, the shape of the deepened module, what sits behind the seam, what tests survive.

Side effects happen inline as decisions crystallize; call the `skill` tool with `domain-model` to keep the domain model current as you go:

- **Naming a deepened module after a concept not in `CONTEXT.md`?** Add the term to `CONTEXT.md`. Create the file lazily if it doesn't exist.
- **Sharpening a fuzzy term during the conversation?** Update `CONTEXT.md` right there.
- **User rejects the candidate with a load-bearing reason?** Offer an ADR, framed as: _"Want me to record this as an ADR so future architecture reviews don't re-suggest it?"_ Only offer when the reason would actually be needed by a future explorer to avoid re-suggesting the same thing; skip ephemeral reasons ("not worth it right now") and self-evident ones.
- **Want to explore alternative interfaces for the deepened module?** Call the `skill` tool with `codebase-design` and use its design-it-twice parallel sub-agent pattern.

# Prototype

A prototype is **throwaway code that answers a question**. The question decides the shape. It is not a first
draft of the feature: no tests, no persistence, no polish, no production path. The decision it settles is the
only thing that survives; the code is captured on a throwaway branch and never merged.

## When this is the right tool

Use it when the question is one of these, and the user agrees:

- **"What should this look like?"** – a structural layout choice: three genuinely different information
  hierarchies, not three colour variants.
- **"Does this logic / state model feel right?"** – a state machine, a set of rules or a data shape pushed
  through cases that are hard to reason about on paper.
- **"How should this flow feel?"** – a sequence a person walks through, where the order and the feedback are
  the question.

Do **not** prototype a question a guideline, the vision or the domain model already answers. Do not prototype
polish (colour, spacing, copy), and do not use it to avoid a grilling decision. The grilling comes first; the
prototype is evidence for one open branch of it.

## Pick a branch

Identify which question is being answered – from the user's prompt, the story, the surrounding code, or by
asking if the user is around:

- **"Does this logic / state model feel right?"** → [LOGIC.md](LOGIC.md). One self-contained HTML file with
  free-play buttons and tabbed guided walkthroughs that push the state model through the awkward cases. A
  non-developer can drive it.
- **"What should this look like?"** → [UI.md](UI.md). Several radically different variants in one
  self-contained HTML file, switchable via a `?variant=` URL search param and a floating bottom bar.

The two branches produce very different artifacts, so getting this wrong wastes the whole prototype. If the
question is genuinely ambiguous and the user isn't reachable, default to whichever branch better matches the
surrounding code (a backend module → logic; a page or component → UI) and state the assumption at the top of
the prototype.

## Where it lives

In discovery, the prototype is **standalone**: `docs/prototypes/<slug>/index.html`, written by the
`ux-designer`, with a short `README.md` next to it (question, branch, variants/scenarios, timebox, verdict).
No application code, no framework, no build step, no shell. The user opens the file in a browser.

A question that genuinely needs the real application – an existing page, real data, the real header and
sidebar – is an **in-app prototype**. That is the exception: it is built by the main session during
`/implement` (see [UI.md](UI.md)), not by the `ux-designer`, and it follows the project's routing convention
with a clearly marked throwaway route. The same capture rules apply.

## Rules that apply to both

1. **Throwaway from day one, and clearly marked as such.** The path or the first line says `PROTOTYPE`. Name
   it so a casual reader cannot mistake it for production.
2. **Trivial to run.** Standalone: double-click the HTML file. In-app: one command from the project's task
   runner. No thinking required to start it.
3. **No persistence by default.** State lives in memory. Persistence is the thing the prototype is *checking*,
   not something it depends on. If the question explicitly involves a database, use a scratch database or a
   local file with a clear "PROTOTYPE, wipe me" name.
4. **Skip the polish.** No tests, no error handling beyond what makes the prototype runnable, no abstractions.
   The point is to learn something fast.
5. **Surface the state.** After every action (logic) or on every variant switch (UI), render the full relevant
   state so the user can see what changed.
6. **One question, one timebox.** Write the question at the top, in the user's language, and agree a timebox
   with the user (one working session is the default). If the timebox expires without an answer, stop and
   record what is known – a second prototype needs a new question, not more polish.
7. **Capture the answer, not the code.** Fold the validated decision into the real artifact – the story's
   `## Context`, `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md` (a G-number when it is a recurring rule) or the domain model.
   Then capture the prototype itself as a **primary source**: commit `docs/prototypes/<slug>/` on a throwaway
   branch `prototype/<slug>`, push it only if the user wants to share it, and return to the branch you were
   on. The branch is never merged. The story carries `Prototype: prototype/<slug> – <question> – <verdict>`.

## How it plugs into the workflow

- **`/feature`** – the UX lens proposes a prototype when the frontier leaves a structural UI, flow or state
  question. The user decides. `--prototype[=ui|logic]` makes it explicit. The verdict goes to the
  `ux-designer` (guidelines) and into the story's `## Context` in the main session, before the stories are reviewed.
- **`/implement`** – only when the user asks (`--prototype`) or a spike's question is a UX/state question. A
  `ui` story whose screen shape is still open was not `ready`; the prototype settles it, then the story goes
  back to `review` if its behaviour changed. The engineering rule holds: never decide a story in the code.
- **The `ux-designer`** owns the skill and builds the standalone prototype. It never writes production code,
  tests or stories. The main session captures the branch and passes the verdict on.

The user has asked for a **retrospective**. You are suggesting improvements to the coding agent's **environment** to improve future runs.

## Steps

1. Call the `skill` tool with `writing-for-agents` for the writing style guide.

2. Read the primary sources for the session the user specifies. This may mean searching through session history on this machine (the current session, or the OpenCode session store under `~/.local/share/opencode/` when running in OpenCode; sessions run on another machine are not there – ask the user). If the user doesn't specify a session, default to the current one.

3. Look for candidates for improvement in these categories.

- **Navigation**: how easy was it for the agent to find the right files? Are there hidden dependencies between files? Would a **navigation pointer** make it easier? _Use when_ the session took a long time to find a piece of information.
- **Automated checks**: are there automated checks that could catch errors the agent made? Linting, typing, tests, filesystem linters? Read the repo's own check command first (its `package.json`/build-tool `lint`/`check` scripts, its CI workflow), so a check that already exists but sits unwired or silently broken is the finding, not a reinvention. A repo with no **guardrail** (no pre-commit hook and no CI job running its lint/typecheck/test command) is itself a finding: an un-linted repo is a standing missed opportunity, not a neutral default. _Use when_ the agent made a mistake an automated check could have caught, or the repo has no guardrail at all.
- **Coding standards**: should the **reviewer agent** be given a new rule to enforce? Should an existing rule be removed or clarified? Classify the violation first: a **mechanical** one (a fixed syntactic pattern, a banned API, an import shape, a file-location rule) gets a deterministic check, full stop: a custom rule in the repo's own linter, a new pre-commit hook, or a new CI job, whichever the repo's language and existing guardrail make cheapest. Default to building the check over writing the rule. Reserve `CODING_STANDARDS.md` for genuine **judgement calls** (cross-file consistency, "matches the surrounding style," anything no guardrail could ever substitute for). _Use when_ the reviewer agent failed to catch a mistake.
- **Global AGENTS.md**: are there any steering instructions that should be moved to coding standards (or automated checks) instead? _Use when_ the AGENTS.md file is particularly large - in the repo OR the user's global scope.
- **Tool economy**: did the agent make expensive tool calls that could be streamlined? Is there any custom tooling (CLI's, MCP's) that is particularly token-inefficient? _Use when_ the agent made an expensive tool call.
- **No-ops**: look for instructions in steering files that don't modify the agent's behavior. _Use when_ the steering files are large and unwieldy.
- **Information access**: look for opportunities to increase the agent's access to information. Teeing dev server logs, readonly access to third-party services. _Use when_ a crucial piece of information was not available to the agent.

4. Present these candidates to the user, in order of severity. Removing or simplifying a rule, check or instruction is a candidate on equal footing with adding one, and "the environment held up, nothing to change" is a complete result. Each candidate names the concrete mistake in the session it would have prevented. The user picks; change nothing before they do.

## Reference

### Implementation vs Review

Remember that all work goes through two stages: implementation and review. The implementation agent has the most **context pressure**. They are responsible for exploration, writing code, and debugging failures.

The review agent has the least context pressure - it receives a diff, so no exploration needed. It often does not need to write code or debug.

This means that the review agent should be responsible for imposing coding standards, not the implementation agent.

### Files

You have access to several files in the repo:

- `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md`: these files are pushed to the context window of any agent working in this repo. They should be used incredibly sparingly, usually only for **navigation pointers** to other files.
- `CODING_STANDARDS.md`: this file is read during review, not implementation. Add **navigation pointers** to docs folders if the standards file gets more than 1,000 lines long.
- Docs: use docs as references files, pointed to by other files. Look for existing docs before writing new ones.
- Skills: use skills for docs (since their description goes into the agent's context window), or for user-invoked commands. Follow the advice in the `writing-for-agents` skill.

### In this project

The files above map onto this repository:

- `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md` when Claude Code is also used) is the always-loaded file.
- The coding standards are `docs/engineering/conventions.md`; the review agents are `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md` and `.opencode/agents/acceptance-tester.md`.
- The check command is `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/verify.ts`; the guardrails are `.claude/hooks/*.ts`, wired for OpenCode in `.opencode/plugins/kataster/index.ts` (and for Claude Code in `.claude/settings.json`), and CI in `.github/workflows/`.
- The rules in `AGENTS.md` bind the retro's proposals too, e.g. the follow-up hurdle and tooling in `.claude/` as TypeScript run directly by Node.

# Story Review

There is no simulated role play. The domain, architecture and testability decisions were made in the grilling and
the event storming; the **spec linter** now checks mechanically that the story carries them. The user approves; the
agent does not approve on their behalf.

1. **Selection**: Stories from the invocation arguments, or all with `status: review` in `docs/stories/`. With a

2. **Lint first** – this is the gate, not a suggestion:

   ```bash
   node .claude/skills/user-stories/scripts/lint-story.ts ST-NNN
   ```

   Errors are the agent's to fix in the story: a missing `aggregate`/`command`, a command that belongs to another
   aggregate, events that are not exactly what the command produces, a missing `Given/When/Then`, more than 4
   scenarios, duplicate titles, a broken reference. Do not weaken a check to get green – if the model is missing the
   event or aggregate, fix `docs/domain/events.yaml` (event-storming/domain-model skill) first.
3. **Warnings that matter**: a `ui: true` story with no empty/rejection case, a legacy `type: story`, a scenario that

   ```bash
   node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/story-status.ts ST-NNN ready-for-human-review
   ```

6. **The user approves** – present one short table (ID, title, type, command/aggregate, scenario count, warnings) and

   ```bash
   node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/story-status.ts ST-NNN ready
   ```

   `review` or `draft` with their reason.
7. **UX on demand only**: a story with `ui: true` may get a component/Figma proposal from the `ux-designer`, but

8. Wrap-up: run `node .claude/skills/user-stories/scripts/lint-story.ts`, show the status overview and point to

# Shape a large idea

This is the step between an idea and `/feature`. It answers four questions and then stops:

1. **Should we do this at all?** Problem, outcome, fit with the vision, non-goals.
2. **Where does it belong?** Existing context, new context, shared library, or cross-cutting.
3. **What does it touch?** What changes, and what is genuinely new.
4. **What does it roughly cost?** Scope, range, risk, confidence – not a single number.

It creates **no stories**. Stories remain `/feature`'s job, one slice at a time.

## When to use it

Use `/shape` when the idea is larger than one feature: it crosses contexts, needs a new context or service, a
migration, an integration, or the question "should we, and what does it cost?" is still open. A normal story goes
straight to `/feature`; don't turn this into ceremony.

A **new service in an existing monorepo** is not greenfield. It inherits the stack, the shared packages, the
deployment and the identity model – treat those as constraints, not as a blank page.

## 0. Intake and mode

A reference (`ST-NNN`, `#123`, `PROJ-123`, URL) is resolved with the read-only intake:

```bash
node .claude/skills/feature/scripts/intake.ts <reference> --json
# Jira: fetch the issue with jira_get_issue, write it as JSON, then
node .claude/skills/feature/scripts/intake.ts PROJ-123 --from <issue.json> --json
```

Summarize the source in 3–5 lines and have the user confirm it. A ticket is **evidence, not a specification**.

`--dry-run` – or the user saying "just walk me through it" – means: grill, show the brief in the conversation,
write **nothing**. Without it, write the artifact only after the user confirms the summary.

## 1. Read and scan

Read `docs/product/vision.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, `docs/domain/events.yaml`, `docs/domain/context-map.md`,
`docs/architecture/data-model.md`, `docs/architecture/repo-map.md`/`.json`, `docs/engineering/conventions.md`,
`docs/adr/`, `docs/stories/BACKLOG.md`, `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md`.

Also scan the **configuration and integration points** for systems that already own the data the idea is about:
`.env.example`, `configuration.ts`, config DTOs, API clients, external ids in entities. A name that appears only
there – a store, an ERP, a marketplace – is evidence of a system the brief must place. Report what you found and
what it implies; do not turn a config key into an architectural decision.

If an analogue exists (a sibling service the idea resembles), use it as evidence. If it is large and not adopted,
delegate one `repo-analyst` lens with a clear task instead of reading all of it yourself. Its model is evidence,
**never** the new context's model.

Three starting points:

- **Domain model exists** (adopted, or after `/bootstrap`): full placement, impact and cost.
- **No domain model**: frame and slice are still useful; placement stays `unknown`; recommend `/bootstrap` or
  `/adopt`. Do not invent contexts from the idea.
- **Partially adopted / an analogue exists**: use the sibling's model where it exists and its code/config where it
  does not. Confidence is `medium` at best; say what is inferred. If the sibling is central, recommend
  `/adopt <sibling>` as the first slice before committing to a cost range.

## 2. Frame – product lens

Call the `grilling` skill. The frontier:

- Which problem, for which user group, and why now?
- What is the observable outcome, and how would we know it worked?
- Must / should / could / won't – what ships first, what is explicitly out?
- Does it fit `vision.md`, or does it change the vision? A vision change is the user's decision.
- What is the cost of **not** doing it – opportunity or fear?
- Constraints: deadline, regulation, budget, team, existing commitments.
- At least one non-goal: what this initiative will not become.

Don't move on before the user confirms a shared understanding.

## 3. Place – architect lens

Call the `architect` skill (and `domain-model` where the language is unclear). For each capability:

| If … | Then |
|---|---|
| same language, same invariants, additive change | **existing context** |
| a term means something else, or a new invariant must be immediately consistent | **new context** |
| different rate of change, team, regulation or external model | **new context** |
| pure logic used by two or more contexts, no lifecycle of its own | **shared library** |
| notifications, audit, auth, files – a generic capability | prefer an **existing generic context** over a new one |

A new **service** is not automatically a new **domain**, and a new domain is not automatically a new service.
Separate contexts can share infrastructure packages; they must not share a domain model just because the words
look alike. Same word, different meaning (Product as dish vs. Product as sellable variant) is the classic reason
to split.

Produce a recommendation **with at least one alternative and its consequence**, plus a confidence:

> Reuse `BC-Delivery` for rescheduling (cheap, but the aggregate grows) vs. a new `BC-Delivery-Planning` (cleaner
> consistency boundary, one more integration). Recommendation: existing context for slice 1, revisit if carriers
> get their own scheduling model.

The user decides.

## 4. Impact – engineering lens

Split the answer into **change** and **build new**. Leave nothing implicit.

| Dimension | Questions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Domain | which aggregates, events, commands, policies, read models? new or changed? | `events.yaml` (IDs, counts) |
| Code | which packages and consumers? which new packages? | `repo-map`, dependency edges |
| Interfaces | screens/forms/flows, API endpoints, jobs, webhooks, integrations | `ux-guidelines`, conventions |
| Data | schema change, migration, backfill, retention, reporting | `data-model.md`, schema |
| Rules | boundaries (`boundaries.yaml`), permissions, checks (`checks.yaml`) | architecture checks |
| Tests | which seams – command, policy, read model, page? | seam catalog |
| Ops | config, deployment, monitoring, support | profile, ADRs |

## 5. Slice

Propose 2–5 independently valuable slices, walking skeleton first. Each slice should be a `/feature` run, not a
project. For each: outcome, contexts touched, dependencies, rough size, confidence.

If the idea cannot be sliced, say so – that is a finding, not a failure of the format.

## 6. Cost

Never one number. Give **scope**, **range** and **risk**, plus the basis.

- **Scope:** number of slices and stories, with sizes (XS–XL). The most defensible unit the toolkit has.
- **Range:** e.g. "3–5 stories, mostly S/M" or "2–4 weeks with one developer". Person-days only if the user has a
  calibration ("1 M ≈ 3 days"); otherwise keep story sizes.
- **Risk:** what could blow the estimate up – unknown integration, migration, compliance, missing language.
- **Confidence:** low/medium/high, and **what would raise it** (spike, prototype, measurement, talking to the
  carrier).
- **Basis:** the counts behind the estimate (e.g. 1 new command, 1 event, 1 policy, 1 read model, 1 page, 1
  migration, 2 packages, 1 integration).
- **Analogue:** if a similar service exists, use it as the calibration anchor – modules, LOC, endpoints, entities,
  specs, and which parts are domain-specific vs. generic. Say what can be reused and what is genuinely new. The
  analogue is evidence, not a template; a copy is not automatically the right design.

Rules: an unknown is a line in the brief, not a silent +20 %. A spike is a cost, not a gap – give it a question and
a timebox. Estimate the **delta** to today's system, not the whole system. Without evidence, say `unknown` and
recommend discovery.

## 7. Decide and write

End with exactly one recommendation:

`go` · `go with slice 1` · `spike first` · `needs discovery (/bootstrap or /adopt)` · `park` · `no-go`

The user decides. Write `docs/product/initiatives/<slug>.md` after the user confirms the summary of steps 2–6.
Set `status: proposed`; only the user sets `accepted`. On handoff, set `promoted: <slug>` and send the first slice
to `/feature`. **Do not create stories here and do not touch `docs/stories/`.**

With `--dry-run`, print the same brief in the conversation and write no file.

### Artifact

```markdown
---
status: proposed          # proposed | accepted | parked | rejected
created: 2026-10-31
source: PROJ-123          # optional
promoted: ""              # feature:<slug> once slices are handed to /feature
---

# Initiative: <title>

## Problem & outcome
## Fit with the vision
## Placement
| Capability | Context | New/existing | Why | Confidence |
## Impact – change vs. build new
| Dimension | Change | New | Evidence |
## Slices
1. …
## Rough cost
| Currency | Estimate | Confidence | Basis |
## Risks & open questions
## Recommendation
```

## Guardrails

- The brief is a proposal. The user sets `accepted`.
- Do not let the estimate become a commitment. It is a range with a basis.
- Every brief ends in a recommendation; do not use `/shape` to avoid a decision.
- Do not turn initiatives into a shadow backlog. They have no `ready`/`done`; only stories do.
- Do not write an artifact when the user only wants to test the method.
- Keep the artifact project-neutral except for the project's own terms from `CONTEXT.md`.
- Never present an analogue's domain model as the new context's model.

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams: where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user – the seam catalog in `docs/engineering/conventions.md` is confirmed already, so only a seam outside it goes to the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?" Give each proposed seam a one-line note on what it catches and what it misses.

When the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the `skill` tool with `codebase-design` for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (the review and refactor steps of `/implement`), not the red → green implementation cycle.

# User Stories

The backlog is **local by default**: every story is a Markdown file in `docs/stories/`, and there is no external
issue tracker. With `backlog.provider` set to `github` or `jira` in `.claude/project.json`, the tracker is the source
of truth and `docs/stories/` is its local mirror – the `backlog` skill owns the sync. In both cases the story file is
the artifact this skill describes, and `docs/stories/BACKLOG.md` is generated from it by a hook – never edit it
manually.

## The spec engineer (main session)

There is no requirements subagent. The main session writes the stories, because it already holds the grilling, the
event storming and the user's decisions – handing them to another agent only adds friction and summary loss
(user, 2026-11-03).

While writing, hold **three lenses at once**:

1. **Domain** – is the behaviour unambiguous? One command, one actor, one observable outcome per scenario. No soft
   wording ("fast", "user-friendly"), no hidden second behaviour.
2. **Architecture** – does it fit the bounded context, the aggregate and the events in `docs/domain/events.yaml`?
   Does the command belong to the aggregate named in the story? Does it need a new event or invariant first?
3. **Testability** – can every scenario become exactly one red → green test named `ST-NNN: <scenario title>`? Is the
   *When* the real entry point and is every *Then* an assertion with a literal from the scenario?

If a lens fails, fix the model (`CONTEXT.md`, `events.yaml`, an ADR) before writing the story. A story that hides an
open decision is a story that will be decided in code.

## The 1-command rule

**One story = one command + the events it produces on one aggregate.** Do not merge several domain commands into one
story to "save a ticket"; that is what made stories unpredictable. A second command is a second story (or a
dependency), not a second scenario set.

Mechanically enforced by the linter for `type: domain`:

- `aggregate: AGG-…` and `command: CMD-…` are required and must exist in `events.yaml`;
- the command must belong to the stated aggregate;
- `events` must be exactly what that command produces – no more, no fewer.

**At most 4 Gherkin scenarios** per domain story: one happy path and up to three edge/error cases. More means the
story merges commands, restates a UX guideline pattern, or should be split.

## Derivation from the Event Storming
| Source in `events.yaml` | typically becomes |
|---|---|
| Actor + command → event | Story "As a <actor>, I want to <command>, so that <effect>" |
| Policy (automatic) | Story from the beneficiary's perspective ("… I am notified when …") |
| Read model | Story about finding/seeing information |
| Hotspot | Spike (question + timebox) or `[OPEN]` in the story |
| External system | Story or task for the integration |

Every domain story links the affected events (`events: [EVT-…]`). Commands without a story = gap → report it.

## File & Frontmatter
File: `docs/stories/ST-NNN-short-title.md` (three-digit number, consecutive, never reused).
Template: `templates/story-template.md`. Schema: `schema/story.schema.json`.

| Field | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id`, `title`, `type`, `status` | yes | identity and workflow state |
| `priority` (`must/should/could/wont`) | yes | backlog order; starts as `should` |
| `aggregate` (`AGG-…`), `command` (`CMD-…`) | for `type: domain` | the 1-command rule, cross-checked against `events.yaml` |
| `events` (`EVT-…`) | for `type: domain` | exactly the command's `produces` |
| `context` (`BC-…`) | for `type: domain` | the bounded context |
| `ui` (`true`) | no | story has a frontend part; triggers the on-demand UX utility |
| `size`, `risk`, `depends_on` | no | optional planning hints; no sizing gate |
| `labels` | no | lowercase, e.g. `mvp`, `feature:<slug>` |
| `external` | with a tracker | backlog sync – never by hand |

With `backlog.provider` = `github` or `jira`, `external` holds the tracker key (`external.key`) and URL. The sync writes
it; a story must have it before it reaches `ready`. `ST-NNN` stays the stable id – never renumber a story to follow an
issue key, and never use a label that starts with the management prefix (`kataster-` by default).

**No implementation foundation inside a domain story** (user, 2026-10-01). A story describes behaviour a person can
observe; technical groundwork that several stories need is its own `task`/`tech-task`, with its own `depends_on`.
A checklist of files to create, layers to convert or configs to set is an implementation plan, not acceptance
criteria – it is neither the user's language nor a testable outcome, and it hides the real size of the story.

## Types: domain, fast lane, tech task, spike

| `type` | Use for | Path in `/implement` |
|---|---|---|
| `domain` (default) | behaviour in the domain model: one command, one aggregate, Gherkin scenarios | full: TDD per scenario, traceability, diff-scaled review |
| `chore` | UI tweak, refactoring, dependency bump, small cleanup | fast lane: no Gherkin matching, no formal reviews |
| `task` | setup or a small non-domain change that is not a chore | fast lane (same as `chore`) |
| `tech-task` | deliberate technical groundwork several stories need, with a checklist | full: checklist evidence + acceptance tester |
| `spike` | a timeboxed question, checklist of what to answer | no TDD; evidence in the checklist |

`chore` and `task` have a `## Task` section and acceptance as a short checklist (`- [ ] …`) or, if they really have
observable behaviour, at most 4 scenarios. They do not need `aggregate`, `command`, `context` or `events`.

`story` is the legacy name of `domain` and still validates. The linter reports it as a warning and relaxes the strict rules
(missing `aggregate`/`command`, more than 4 scenarios) so an upgrade does not turn an existing backlog red – new work
uses `domain`.

## The `ui` flag

`ui: true` marks a story with a frontend part – a screen, a form, a flow a person walks through. It is the **only**
trigger for the on-demand `ux-designer`: component/layout proposals, Figma/design-token logic or a prototype. The UX
utility never gates the story; a missing decision comes back as a proposal, not as a blocker.

The old `labels: [ui]` is still recognised as equivalent. New stories set the flag.

## Status Workflow
`draft` (in progress) → `review` (written, waiting for the linter) → `ready-for-human-review` (spec linter green) →
`ready` (the user approved it) → `in-progress` → `done`.

- **The linter is the gate**: `node .claude/skills/user-stories/scripts/lint-story.ts <file>`. Only when it is green
  does the story move to `ready-for-human-review`; there is no LLM review pass before implementation.
- **`ready` is the user's decision**, not the agent's.
- Discovery ends at `ready`. The engineering workflow (`/implement`) sets `in-progress` and `done` with
  `node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/story-status.ts`; the validation hook enforces the same rules when the file
  is edited directly.
- `in-progress` and `done` need all `depends_on` stories `done`.
- `done` for a domain story needs a test titled `ST-NNN: <scenario title>` for every scenario; for a chore, task,
  tech task or spike every checklist item is ticked `- [x]`.
- A story that turns out wrong during implementation goes from `in-progress` (or `ready`) back to `review`, with
  `[OPEN]` + an entry in `OPEN_QUESTIONS.md`; the main session revises it and the linter/approval runs again.
- `done` is final. A change to finished behaviour is a new story.
- `superseded` – a story that is not built as written, before it was started: its work was done elsewhere (a direct
  change, another story), or a new planning replaces it. Set from `draft`, `review`, `ready-for-human-review` or
  `ready`, never from `in-progress`. Its first paragraph says where the work went or what replaces it; the file stays
  as the record other documents link to. Final like `done`, listed in its own section of the backlog and counted in
  no progress (user, 2026-10-25).

## Body Structure
```
## Story
As a <role from CONTEXT.md>, I want <goal>, so that <business benefit>.

## Context
Briefly: trigger, preconditions, business rules – from the command's `rules` **and from the `invariants` of its
aggregate**. An invariant is stated once, on the aggregate, and a command's `rules` list only what
it adds beyond them (`docs/domain/events.yaml`). So a command with few rules is not a command with
few rules to test: read its aggregate's `invariants` and give every one the command can violate its own rejection
scenario. "A product always has a name, a price and exactly one category" is why
`CMD-CorrectProduct` needs a scenario for an emptied name, although its `rules` do not mention it.

## Acceptance Criteria
Scenario: <Happy path>
  Given …
  When …
  Then …

Scenario: <Error or edge case>
  …

## Out of Scope
## Open Questions
```
Scenario titles are unique within a story and become test titles (`ST-NNN: <scenario title>`). Renaming a scenario
of an `in-progress` or `done` story breaks that link – the test must be renamed too (`verify.ts` reports it).

Chore/task/tech-task: `## Task`, `## Acceptance Criteria` (checklist `- [ ] …`).
Spike: `## Question`, `## Timebox`, `## Acceptance Criteria` (checklist).

## Quality Rules
- **INVEST**: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable.
- Gherkin in English (`Given / When / Then`); every scenario has all three steps. At least a happy path + one
  error/edge case, at most 4 scenarios.
- Scenarios describe **behavior**, not UI details ("clicks the blue button" ✗) and not technology.
- Spend the scenarios on domain behavior and real rejections. A pattern `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md` already
  defines (grouping, collapsing, kept choices after a rejection) is a G-number in the Context, tested once where the
  pattern is built, not restated as scenarios.
- Measurable outcomes: "Then the item has the status 'out of order'" instead of "Then it works".
- Non-functional requirements as concrete scenarios or checklist items with a number.
- Terms exactly as in the glossary `CONTEXT.md`; never use an `_Avoid_` synonym.

## Splitting Patterns (one command per story)
By command · by business rule · happy path first, special cases later · by data variant · by role ·
"manual first, automated later". If two commands share a screen, that is two stories and one `depends_on`, not one
story with two `When`s.

## Validation (deterministic, no LLM)
The spec linter is the gate before `ready-for-human-review`:

```bash
node .claude/skills/user-stories/scripts/lint-story.ts            # all stories
node .claude/skills/user-stories/scripts/lint-story.ts ST-012     # one story
kataster lint-story docs/stories/ST-012-*.md                      # from the CLI
```

It checks frontmatter syntax and required fields, the aggregate/command/event cross-check against
`docs/domain/events.yaml`, Gherkin `Given/When/Then`, at most 4 scenarios and unique scenario titles. A PostToolUse
hook runs the same rules after every write and regenerates `BACKLOG.md`; `verify.ts` runs them for the whole backlog.

After deleting or renaming story files, regenerate the backlog:
`node .claude/skills/user-stories/scripts/render-backlog.ts`

With a tracker, validation also refuses a `ready`, `in-progress` or `done` story without `external`, and warns about
labels reserved for the sync. Pull before validating a mirror that may be stale (`/backlog-sync pull`) and push after
changing it (`/backlog-sync push`).

# UX Design

This skill is **how** we decide the interface. **What** we decided is `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md` – the
yardstick, owned by the `ux-designer` agent, approved by the user. The two are not interchangeable: a judgement
that is not in the guidelines is an opinion, and the next story will contradict it.

The technical side lives elsewhere and is not repeated here: `docs/engineering/conventions.md` (page frames,
design size, component rules, where message catalogs live) and the ADRs. Point at those, don't restate them.

## Who we are designing for

`docs/product/vision.md` is the source – read it, don't paraphrase it from memory. The user groups, their
devices, their situation and the non-goals are all there; every decision is measured against them. If the vision
does not name them yet, that is the first thing to grill, not something to invent.

Three questions the vision must answer before the interface can be judged:

- **Who is in front of the screen, and in what situation?** Standing, walking, one hand, gloves, noisy, rushed,
  at a desk. How long may the task take before it is a failure?
- **On what?** Phone, tablet, desktop, kiosk. What is the design size – the size the layout is built for, not the
  exception?
- **What can they not rely on?** No account, no connectivity, no training, no second language, no patience.

`.claude/project.json` holds the UI language (`languages.ui`). Every term's UI wording lives in `CONTEXT.md` as a
`_UI (<lang>)_` line; the UI uses exactly that word, never a synonym.

## When a feature has a frontend part

Assume it does. The exceptions are a policy, a migration, a pure read model with no page of its own, and tooling.
Everything else a person triggers has a screen, and if nobody designs it, it gets designed by accident.

**The test, during grilling:** can you name the screen a person is on when this happens, what they see before they
act, and what they see afterwards? If any of the three is unclear, the feature has an open UX question – raise it
in the grilling round, don't settle it while writing code.

Stories with a frontend part carry **`ui: true`** (the legacy label `ui` is still recognised). It is the trigger for
the on-demand `ux-designer` – component/layout proposals, Figma/design-token logic, a prototype – and for the UI
warnings in the spec linter. It is not a gate: a missing flag means a story nobody looks at from this side, not a
story that cannot ship.

## The UX frontier – what to grill

Ask these in the grilling round of `/feature` (or `/grill-with-docs`), each with a recommended answer, as the
`grilling` skill requires. They belong to the round whose prerequisites are settled – the purpose of a screen
cannot be asked before the domain decision it serves.

1. **Entry.** How does the person get here – QR code, navigation, a link from another screen, a dashboard? Is this
   a destination or a step in a flow?
2. **The one job.** What is the single thing this screen exists for? If there are two, say why they are not two
   screens.
3. **Before acting.** What does the person need to see to decide – and what can be left out? Name what is *not*
   shown; a screen that shows everything decides nothing.
4. **The action.** How many taps from arriving to done? What is the default, so the common case needs no input?
5. **Afterwards.** Where does the person land, and how do they know it worked? (Here: a redirect plus the changed
   list, or a confirmation – see the guidelines.)
6. **When it goes wrong.** Which rejections can the command return, what does each one say in the UI language, and does the
   typed input survive? Every error code of the command needs a text in the catalog – the type check enforces it,
   but the *wording* is a UX decision.
7. **The empty case.** What does the screen show when there is nothing yet – and does it say what to do about it?
8. **The full case.** What happens at 50 items, 200 open records, a 60-character name, a three-line title?
   Which of these is realistic for these users, and which is not worth designing for?
9. **Permission.** What does someone who may not do this see – the screen without the action, or not the screen?
10. **Language.** Which UI language(s) apply (see `.claude/project.json`), which domain terms appear, and do they match
    `CONTEXT.md`'s `_UI (<lang>)_` wording exactly?

A question whose answer is already in `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md` is not asked again – quote the guideline
instead. That is what makes the yardstick pay off.

## When paper is not enough – the prototype

Most UX questions are settled in words: entry, job, states, wording. A few are not – which of three
structurally different layouts works, or whether a state model still feels right once it is pushed through the
awkward cases. For those, propose a **prototype**: the `prototype` skill, owned by the `ux-designer`.

Propose it in the grilling round, with a recommended answer, when the question is:

- a structural layout choice (not colour, spacing or copy),
- a state model or a flow that is hard to reason about on paper,
- a screen that does not exist yet and whose shape decides how the stories are cut.

Do not propose one for polish, or for a question a guideline or the vision already answers. State the one
question, the branch (`ui` or `logic`), the variants or scenarios, and the timebox. The user decides.

The verdict goes into `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md` as a G-number when it is a recurring rule, and into the
story's `## Context` (`Prototype: prototype/<slug> – <question> – <verdict>`). The prototype itself is
throwaway: it lives under `docs/prototypes/<slug>/`, is captured on a throwaway branch, and is never merged.
Details: `.claude/skills/prototype/SKILL.md`.

At story review, a `ui: true` story whose screen shape is still open is not `ready`: send it back to `/feature` for a
prototype (or a spike), rather than approving it and deciding it in code. The `ux-designer` advises; the user
approves.

## What goes into the story, and what does not

Stories stay at the level of observable behaviour. No implementation detail in a story: no markup, no pixel values.
Component proposals belong to the `ux-designer` reply and the engineering conventions, not to the story.

- **Into the Gherkin**: what a person sees and can do, in terms a test can check. "Then the open cases of the
  item are listed, newest first" – yes. "Then a card component with a muted description is rendered" – no.
- **Into `## Context`**: the screen's one job, the entry point, the states that have to exist (empty, rejected, no
  permission), and the UI wording decided during grilling.
- **A scenario for the empty case and for the rejection**, when the story introduces a screen. These are the two
  that get forgotten, and they are the ones a person actually meets.
- **Not into the story**: layout, component choice, spacing, colour. Those follow from the guidelines and the
  engineering conventions; if a story needs to say them, the guidelines are missing something – say so.

## Reviewing a screen that exists

Against `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md`, in this order – stop at the first level that fails, the ones below it do
not matter yet:

1. **Can the person do the job at all**, at the design size, without JavaScript where the conventions require it?
2. **Do they understand what they are looking at** – heading, what each number means, which item or case this is about?
3. **Do the four states exist** – empty, full, rejected, no permission?
4. **Is the language right** – glossary wording, in the UI language, sounding like the domain and not like a database?
5. **Is it consistent** with the screens that already exist – same patterns, same words for the same thing?
6. Only then: proportion, rhythm, polish.

Report findings the way a code review does: what, where, why it matters, and what you would do instead. Never
"this feels unpolished" – name the decision that is wrong.

## Keeping the yardstick honest

Every decision the user approves goes into `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md` immediately, in the voice of a rule
("A form that is rejected keeps what was typed and names the reason above the submit button"), with the date and
the reason. A guideline nobody can point at is not a guideline. When the code and the guidelines disagree, raise
it – don't silently follow either.

# Skill mechanics

The skill-specific branch of [`writing-for-agents`](SKILL.md): what changes when the document is a skill (frontmatter, the invocation choice, and router skills). Everything else about writing it is the universal reference in `SKILL.md`.

## Invocation

Two choices, trading the two loads:

- A **model-invoked** skill keeps a `description`, so the agent can fire it autonomously, and other skills can reach it. You can still type its name: model-invocation always _includes_ user reach; a description only ever adds agent discovery, never removes the human's. The description is the skill's top-level context pointer, forced to stay loaded at all times: permanent context load in exchange for discoverability. A model-invoked skill whose content is all reference is also one home for shared reference: another skill can invoke it, so reference needed by several skills lives in one place. Mechanics: omit `disable-model-invocation`, and write a model-facing description carrying the trigger branches (the pointer-writing rules in `SKILL.md` apply in full).
- A **user-invoked** skill strips the description from the agent's reach: only the human typing its name can invoke it, and no other skill can. Zero context load, but it spends cognitive load: you are the index that must remember it exists. Mechanics: set `disable-model-invocation: true`; the `description` becomes human-facing: a one-line summary, trigger lists stripped.

Pick model-invocation only when the agent must reach the skill on its own, or another skill must. If it only ever fires by hand, make it user-invoked and pay no context load.

Shared reference that two user-invoked skills both need can live in neither: with no descriptions, neither can fire the other. Push it to a plain file outside the skill system: external reference any skill can point at.

## Splitting by invocation

The invocation cut of splitting (the sequence cut lives in `SKILL.md`): split off a model-invoked skill when you have a distinct leading word that should trigger it on its own (a trigger word you actually use in your prompts), or another skill must reach it. You pay context load for the new always-loaded description, so that independent reach has to be worth it.

## Router skills

When user-invoked skills multiply past what you can remember, that piled-up cognitive load is cured by a **router skill**: one user-invoked skill that names the others and when to reach for each, so the human has one skill to remember instead of many. It can only hint, never fire them: user-invoked skills have no description, so nothing but the human can reach them.
