Reference for writing any document an agent consumes: a skill, an `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`, a doc reached by a pointer. The packaging differs; the writing does not: the same levers make each one predictable, since the agent takes the same _process_ every run rather than producing the same output.

When the document you're writing is a skill, read [`SKILL-MECHANICS.md`](SKILL-MECHANICS.md) for frontmatter, invocation choice, and router skills.

## Context pointers

A **context pointer** is a reference held in the agent's context that names some out-of-context material and encodes the condition for reaching it. A skill's description is one; a line in `AGENTS.md` naming a doc is the same object. The pointer's _wording_, not its target, decides when the agent reaches the material, and how reliably. A must-have target behind a weakly worded pointer is a variance bug: sharpen the wording first, and inline the material only if sharpening fails.

A pointer does two jobs: state what the material is, and list the **branches** that should trigger reaching it (a branch is a distinct case the document handles, so different runs take different paths through it). Every word of an always-loaded pointer costs on every turn, so it earns even harder pruning than the body:

- **Front-load the leading word**: the pointer is where it does its triggering work.
- **One trigger per branch.** Synonyms that rename a single branch are one branch written twice; collapse them and keep only genuinely distinct branches.
- **Cut identity the body already carries.**

## The two loads

Every document and pointer you add spends one of two budgets:

- **Context load** is the cost of always-loaded material on the agent's window: an `AGENTS.md` line, a skill description, anything sitting in context every turn, spending tokens and attention whether or not it fires.
- **Cognitive load** is the cost on the human: which documents exist and when to reach for each. The human is the index. Not a cost to minimise: it is the price of human agency; spend it where human judgement matters, remove it where it does not.

Material reached only through a pointer escapes context load at the price of the pointer's own line; material with no pointer at all rides entirely on cognitive load.

## Information hierarchy

A document is built from two content types: **steps** (the ordered actions the agent performs) and **reference** (definitions, rules, facts consulted on demand). The two mix freely: all steps (a recipe), all reference (a review's rules, this skill), or both. The core decision is where each piece sits on the **information hierarchy**, a ladder ranked by how immediately the agent needs the material:

1. **In-file step** is the primary tier: what the agent does, in order.
2. **In-file reference** is consulted on demand. Often a legitimately flat peer-set (every rule of a review on one rung), which is a fine arrangement, not a smell.
3. **Disclosed reference** is pushed out into a separate file, reached by a context pointer, loaded only when the pointer fires. Spans a sibling file in the same folder through fully external reference that lives anywhere and any document can point at.

Push too little down and the top bloats; push too much and you hide material the agent actually needs. That tension is the whole decision.

**Progressive disclosure** is the move down the ladder (out of the main file and behind a pointer) so the top stays legible. Not primarily a token optimisation: it is how the hierarchy is protected. Branching is the cleanest disclosure test: inline what every branch needs, and push behind a pointer what only some branches reach. When a document has steps, in-file reference that should be disclosed buries them and turns attending to them into a coin-flip: a variance lever, not just a legibility one.

**Co-location** is the within-file companion: where the ladder decides _how far down_ a piece sits, co-location decides _what sits beside it_ once there. Keep a concept's definition, rules, and caveats under one heading rather than scattered, so reading one part brings its neighbours with it. The test: the document should read like documentation written for the agent. Grouped material reads that way; scattered material does not. (Distinct from duplication: that repeats one meaning in two places; scattering fragments one meaning across many.)

**Sprawl** is the failure mode here: a document simply too long, even when every line is live and unique. Attention thins across the excess, and every extra line is one more to keep relevant. The cure is the ladder: disclose reference behind pointers, and split by branch or sequence so each path carries only what it needs.

## Steps and completion criteria

Every step ends on a **completion criterion**, the condition that tells the agent the work is done. Two properties make it a lever:

- **Clarity**: can the agent tell done from not-done? A vague bound ("understanding reached") invites **premature completion**: ending the step before it is genuinely done, attention slipping to _being done_. The visible steps still ahead (the **post-completion steps**) supply the pull; the criterion's clarity is the resistance. Defend in order: **sharpen the bound first** (local and cheap); only if it is irreducibly fuzzy _and_ you observe the rush, hide the later steps by splitting the sequence. Hiding only works across a real context boundary (a hand-off or a subagent dispatch; an inline call leaves the later steps in context and clears nothing).
- **Demand**: how much it requires. "Every modified model accounted for" forces thorough work where "produce a change list" does not. Demand drives **legwork** (the digging the agent does within the work, latent in the wording rather than written as its own step), and it is not step-bound: "every rule applied" binds a body of flat reference just as "every step done" binds a sequence, which is how an all-reference document still carries an exhaustiveness bar.

The strongest criteria are both checkable and exhaustive.

## When to split

Splitting one document into two spends one of the two loads, so split only when the cut earns it:

- **By sequence**: split a run of steps where the post-completion steps tempt the agent to rush the one in front of it. Keeping them out of view drives more legwork on the current task. Beware the reverse: merging sequences exposes each step's later steps to what follows, inviting premature completion.
- **By invocation**, skill-specific: see [`SKILL-MECHANICS.md`](SKILL-MECHANICS.md).

## Leading words

A **leading word** is a compact concept already living in the model's pretraining that the agent thinks with while running the document (_lesson_, _fog of war_, _tracer bullets_). Repeated as a token, never as a sentence, it accumulates a distributed definition and anchors a whole region of behaviour in the fewest tokens, by recruiting priors the model already holds. Coining your own works if you define it clearly, but a made-up word recruits no priors: you pay in definition tokens what a pretrained word gives free; reach for an existing word first.

It anchors twice. In the body, _execution_: the agent reaches for the same behaviour every time the word appears, and inside flat reference it focuses attention on a class of thing to look for. In a pointer, _invocation_: when the same word lives in your prompts, your docs, and your codebase, the agent links that shared language to the material and reaches it more reliably.

Hunt for opportunities to refactor with leading words. A triad spelled out at three sites, a pointer spending a sentence to gesture at one idea. Each is a passage begging to collapse into a single token:

- "fast, deterministic, low-overhead" → _tight_ (a _tight_ loop).
- "a loop you believe in" → _red_, turning a fuzzy gate into a binary observable state (the loop goes _red_ on the bug, or it doesn't).

You win twice: fewer tokens, and a sharper hook for the agent to hang its thinking on. Assume every document is carrying restatements that leading words retire. Go find them.

**Negation** is the failure mode beside this lever: steering by prohibition drags the forbidden behaviour into context and makes it _more_ available, not less. _Don't think of an elephant_, and the elephant is all there is; the negation is a weak modifier the strongly-activated concept overruns, so the ban half-reads as an instruction to do the thing. Prompt the **positive**: state the target behaviour ("write one-line comments") so the banned one is never spoken. A prohibition earns its place only as a hard guardrail you cannot phrase positively; even then, pair it with the positive target so attention lands on what to do.

## Pruning

- Keep each meaning in a **single source of truth**: one authoritative place, so changing the behaviour is a one-place edit. **Duplication** (the same meaning in more than one place) costs maintenance and tokens, and inflates a meaning's prominence on the ladder past its real rank. (The accidental inverse of a leading word, which repeats a token on purpose, never the meaning.)
- The **environment** is a source of truth too (`package.json` scripts, config files, the directory layout, `--help` output), and a document that restates it is a **cache**: a copy of a lookup, earning its load only when the lookup is expensive. Cache what the agent cannot find by looking: the unwritten convention, the reason behind a choice, the gotcha no config confesses. Leave the one-file, one-command lookups to the environment, where they cannot go stale.
- Check every line for **relevance**: does it still bear on what the document does? A line loses relevance by never bearing on the task (mere exposition, or a branch that should be disclosed) or by going stale as the behaviour or world it describes changes. Shorter documents are easier to keep relevant. Without a pruning discipline the default fate is **sediment**: stale layers that settle because adding feels safe and removing feels risky, until you must core down through them to find what is still live.
- Hunt **no-ops** sentence by sentence: an instruction the model already obeys by default pays load to say nothing. The test (does it change behaviour versus the default?) is model-relative, not reader-relative: two people disagreeing about a no-op disagree about the default, and settle it by running the document, not by debate. When a sentence fails, delete the whole sentence rather than trim words from it. The test also grades leading words: a word too weak to beat the default (_be thorough_ when the agent is already thorough-ish) is a no-op, and the fix is a stronger word (_relentless_), not a different technique.

# Kataster

**An agent workflow for domain-driven discovery and delivery.** Drop it into a repository, and the agent builds the
domain with you – by grilling, not by guessing – then carries it through stories, test-first implementation and
review.

The name is the German word for the official register of land parcels and their boundaries – a map that is
maintained, not invented. The domain model is that register: bounded contexts are the parcels, the glossary and the
data model are the entries, and nothing goes in without evidence.

Works in two situations:

- **Brownfield** – the repository already has code. `/adopt` analyses code, docs, tests, schema and git history,
  drafts the domain model with evidence, and grills you to correct it. No rewrite, no invented domain.
- **Greenfield** – nothing but an idea. `/bootstrap` grills the vision, runs an event storming, builds contexts,
  aggregates, the data model and the ADRs, and derives the foundation stories and first vertical slice.

The same workflow then handles every large idea (`/shape`), every feature (`/feature`), every story review
(`/review-stories`), implementation (`/implement`) and backlog care (`/groom-backlog`, `/retro`).

```bash
npx kataster init
```

That is the whole installation. It writes `.claude/`, `.opencode/`, `AGENTS.md` and a `docs/` skeleton into the
current repository, detects the stack, and asks four questions – the last one is whether stories stay local or live
in GitHub Issues or Jira (and if so, for the project or repository).

---

## Why this exists

Agents are good at writing code and bad at knowing what the words mean. A repository without a domain model produces
code that is locally plausible and globally inconsistent: three names for one concept, rules enforced only in the UI,
features nobody can place. Kataster makes the domain a first-class artifact – glossary, events, contexts,
aggregates, invariants – and makes the agent earn every statement in it from the user or from evidence.

Two rules run through everything:

1. **Facts are the agent's job, decisions are the user's.** The agent looks things up; it never invents a domain
   term, a rule or a boundary.
2. **The user confirms, the agent writes.** Grilling works in rounds on the *frontier*: every question whose
   prerequisites are settled, each with a recommended answer. Nothing is assumed silently.

## Requirements

- Node.js **22.18+** (the tooling runs TypeScript directly, no build step)
- Git
- An agent harness: **OpenCode** or **Claude Code**
- Optional: `gh` for pull requests and a GitHub Issues backlog, the `mcp-atlassian` MCP server for a Jira backlog,
  a preview provider (Vercel, Netlify, …) for acceptance testing

```bash
# existing repository
npx kataster init --brownfield
# new project
npx kataster init --greenfield
# stories in GitHub Issues or Jira
npx kataster init --backlog github --github-repo acme/shop
npx kataster init --backlog jira --jira-project PROJ
```

Then open the repository in your agent harness and run `/adopt` or `/bootstrap`.

Non-interactive (CI, scripts):

## The commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/adopt [scope] [--stories]` | Brownfield: repository map → one slice (domain + shared library) → evidence → grilling → package docs and checks → gap register; stories only with `--stories`; repeat per slice |
| `/bootstrap` | Greenfield: vision → event storming → domain model → architecture → UX → foundation stories |
| `/grill-me` | Relentless interview on a plan, decision or idea |
| `/grill-with-docs` | The same, writing glossary and ADRs as you go |
| `/event-storming [process]` | Big-picture or single-process event storming |
| `/feature <idea \| ST-NNN \| #123 \| PROJ-123>` | New feature from an idea, an existing story or a ticket: intake and routing, grilling, focused storming, model, stories, review; bugs become a regression story; `--prototype` adds a throwaway prototype before the stories |
| `/shape <idea \| ticket> [--dry-run]` | Before a large feature: frame, place (existing/new context, shared library), impact, slices, rough cost range, recommendation; creates no stories |
| `/review-stories [ST-…]` | Spec linter gate → `ready-for-human-review`; the user approves `ready` |
| `/backlog-sync [status\|pull\|push]` | Keep `docs/stories/` in sync with GitHub Issues or Jira |
| `/groom-backlog [scope]` | Periodic challenge: is this backlog still worth building? |
| `/implement [ST-NNN] [--fast]` | One story on its branch: domain = test-first, diff-scaled review, acceptance; `chore`/`task` or `--fast` = fast lane without Gherkin matching or formal reviews; `--prototype` settles an open UI question first |
| `/improve-codebase-architecture` | Scan for deepening opportunities, present them, grill one |
| `/retro` | Retrospective on a session, proposing rule changes |

### Spec-driven stories, fast lane

Stories are written by the main session as a **spec engineer**, not by simulated roles. Three lenses at once –
domain, architecture, testability – and one mechanical rule: **one story = one command + its events on one
aggregate**, at most four Gherkin scenarios. `aggregate` and `command` are required frontmatter and are cross-checked
against `docs/domain/events.yaml`.

The **spec linter** is the gate and costs no LLM tokens:

```bash
kataster lint-story                      # all stories
kataster lint-story ST-012               # one story
node .claude/skills/user-stories/scripts/lint-story.ts docs/stories/ST-012-*.md
```

Frontmatter and required fields, aggregate/command/event references, Gherkin `Given/When/Then`, the scenario limit
and unique titles. Green → `ready-for-human-review`; only you approve `ready`. The same rules run in the PostToolUse
hook and in `verify.ts`.

Non-domain work takes the **fast lane**: `type: chore` (UI tweak, refactor, dependency) or `type: task` (setup).
`/implement` detects it (or takes `--fast`) and does branch → implement → lint/typecheck/unit tests → PR, without
Gherkin matching or formal review agents. `type: tech-task` keeps its checklist and acceptance; `type: spike` is a
timeboxed question.

### Starting from a ticket

`/feature` also accepts a reference: `/feature #123` (GitHub), `/feature PROJ-123` (Jira, with the issue fetched
through MCP), `/feature https://…` or `/feature ST-042`. A read-only intake resolves it and returns a route: an
existing `draft`/`review` story is revised, a `ready`/`in-progress` one goes to `/implement`, a finished one becomes a
new story, and a bug becomes one regression story instead of a feature. The ticket is **evidence, not a
specification** – its acceptance criteria are grilled, contradictions with the model are findings, and the source is
recorded in each story. `external` is still written only by the backlog sync.

### Shaping a large idea

`/shape` is the step between an idea and `/feature`. It grills the problem, decides where the work belongs – an
existing bounded context, a new one, or a shared library – maps what changes vs. what is built new, proposes 2–5
slices, and gives a rough **cost range with confidence and basis**. It ends with one recommendation: go, go with
slice 1, spike first, needs discovery, park or no-go. It creates **no stories**; each slice goes to `/feature`.

```bash
/shape "shop products with variants and channel prices"
/shape PROJ-123
/shape --dry-run "a new service next to the existing one"   # test the method, write nothing
```

The brief lands in `docs/product/initiatives/<slug>.md` (`proposed` until you accept it). A new service in an
existing monorepo is treated as a new context in an existing landscape, not as a greenfield project; a similar
service is used as evidence and as the cost anchor, never as a template.

### Prototyping an open question

When a UI, flow or state question cannot be settled on paper, `/feature --prototype` (or a proposal from the UX
lens during grilling) runs a throwaway prototype before the stories are written. The `ux-designer` builds one
self-contained HTML file under `docs/prototypes/<slug>/` – several structurally different UI variants or a
clickable state model. The verdict goes into the story and, when it is a recurring rule, into the UX guidelines;
the prototype is captured on a throwaway branch and never merged. `/implement --prototype` does the same for an
open UI question during engineering; if the prototype changes the story, the story goes back to `review`.

```bash
/feature "checkout with saved cards" --prototype=ui
/feature PROJ-123 --prototype=logic
/implement ST-042 --prototype
```

## Greenfield, end to end

1. `npx kataster init --greenfield` → review `.claude/project.json`.
2. `/bootstrap` → vision grilled, event storming, contexts/aggregates/data model, tech-stack ADR, UX guidelines.
3. `/review-stories` → the spec linter turns finished stories into `ready-for-human-review`; you approve `ready`.
4. `/implement` → one story at a time, test-first, reviewed, merged by you.
5. `/feature <idea>` for everything after that.

## Brownfield, end to end

1. `npx kataster init --brownfield` → the profile is filled from the detected stack and monorepo tooling
   (`repo.tooling`: Nx, Turborepo, Bazel, workspaces, Go, Cargo, Gradle, Maven).
2. `/adopt` → a deterministic **repository map** (`docs/architecture/repo-map.md`, `.json`) with packages,
   dependency edges, consumers and an adoption ranking. No questions, no hand-scanning.
3. `/adopt [scope]` → **one slice** (one domain plus at most one shared library): two or three `repo-analyst`
   subagents return evidence (five lenses for a small single-package repository); the main session drafts `CONTEXT.md`, `events.yaml`, context map, as-is data model,
   conventions and de-facto ADRs; it writes `<package>/AGENTS.md` + `<package>/CLAUDE.md`, then grills you.
4. The safety net turns confirmed rules into checks (types, lint/boundary, tests, hooks) – report-only with a
   baseline first, so a brownfield repository does not start red.
5. The gap analysis records **contradictions, missing behaviour and dead code** in the adoption report. It creates
   **no stories by default** – what already works is documented, not re-storied. `/adopt <scope> --stories` turns
   the selected gaps into a backlog when you want one.
6. `/adopt <next path>` for the next slice; `/adopt <scope> --stories`, `/review-stories`, then `/implement`.

Adopt in slices: one bounded context completely beats the whole repository shallowly. The root `AGENTS.md` stays
free of domain; the package docs are loaded only when someone works in that package.

## Monorepos

The installer detects the build tool (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel, pnpm/npm/yarn workspaces, Go, Cargo, Gradle, Maven)
and stores it in `.claude/project.json` → `repo.tooling`. `/adopt` builds the repository map once, then adopts
**one domain plus at most one shared library per session**. Every adopted package gets an `AGENTS.md` with its
purpose, entities or public API, interfaces and pitfalls – plus a one-line `CLAUDE.md` so Claude Code loads it on
demand; OpenCode loads the nested `AGENTS.md` itself. The root `AGENTS.md` stays short and free of domain.

Commands use the detected tool instead of assuming a single package: `nx affected -t test`,
`turbo run test --filter=<package>`, `bazel test //<package>/...`, `pnpm --filter <package> test`. The map also
stores the tool's own graph – Turborepo via `turbo run <task> --dry=json`, Nx via `nx graph`, Bazel from the
`BUILD` deps – and `affected.ts` turns changed files into the affected packages plus the native filter command,
following shared-library dependents:

```bash
node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/affected.ts --changed libs/shared-kernel/src/index.ts
node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/affected.ts --base origin/main
```

## Backlog backends

Stories live in one of three places, chosen at install with `--backlog` and stored in `.claude/project.json`:

| Provider | Source of truth | Transport |
|---|---|---|
| `local` (default) | `docs/stories/` | the Markdown files |
| `github` | GitHub Issues | `gh` CLI – deterministic, works from scripts |
| `jira` | Jira | `mcp-atlassian` – MCP is agent-only |

With a tracker, **the tracker leads** and `docs/stories/` is a synchronized local mirror. That keeps the deterministic
parts – validation, `BACKLOG.md`, scenario ↔ test traceability, `next-story` – working offline, while the team works in
the tracker.

- Each story keeps its stable `ST-NNN` id; the tracker key lives in `external: { provider, key, url }`. Test titles do
  not change.
- Only the backlog core syncs: story content, status, priority, size, risk, context, type, dependencies and labels.
  Reviews and `OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` stay local.
- A story must be linked before it reaches `ready` – the validator refuses an unlinked mirror story.
- On a conflict the tracker wins; the local file is backed up to `.kataster/backup/backlog/` first. GitHub's `push`
  refuses a story whose remote side changed; the Jira plan cannot see Jira, so pull before planning a push.
- GitHub issues are closed for `done`/`superseded`; Jira uses the configured status names and transitions.

```bash
node .claude/skills/backlog/scripts/backlog-status.ts   # what is linked, what drifted
node .claude/skills/backlog/scripts/backlog-push.ts     # mirror → tracker (GitHub)
node .claude/skills/backlog/scripts/backlog-pull.ts     # tracker → mirror (GitHub)
```

For Jira, `jira-plan.ts` prints the exact MCP calls, `jira-record.ts` writes the returned keys back, and
`backlog-pull.ts --from issues.json` imports what the agent fetched through MCP. The `backlog` skill has the full flow.

## Quality gates

- **Hooks** validate `docs/domain/events.yaml` and stories after every write, format and lint changed code, block
  edits to generated files and accepted ADRs, and stop force pushes, production deploys and destructive database
  commands.
- **Path-scoped rules** live in `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths:` frontmatter – for patterns a directory cannot
  express. Claude Code loads them natively; in OpenCode the plugin attaches the matching rule to the session as
  soon as a file under its globs is read or written, so one file serves both harnesses.
- **Architecture boundaries** are data: `docs/architecture/boundaries.yaml` lists allowed/forbidden edges (first
  match wins), `boundary-check.ts` enforces them, and `boundaries.baseline.json` freezes existing debt so only
  new violations fail. `docs/engineering/checks.yaml` decides what runs at edit time and at Stop/CI; the
  `project-check.ts` dispatcher is wired once, not per package.

  ```bash
  node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/boundary-check.ts --init
  node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/boundary-check.ts            # fail on new violations
  node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/boundary-check.ts --update-baseline
  ```
- **`verify.ts`** is the one gate: project checks, artifact validity, scenario ↔ test traceability, domain IDs in
  the code, glossary language.
- **Review agents** never write code or stories: `code-reviewer` and `acceptance-tester` report findings, the
  acceptance verdict decides whether a domain story is `done`, and a finding is fixed in the story or handed back
  as an open question. `ux-designer` is an on-demand utility (`ui: true`), never a gate.

## Upgrading

```bash
npx kataster upgrade
npx kataster doctor
```

`upgrade` replaces workflow files, keeps project content (`CONTEXT.md`, `docs/`, `project.json`) and refuses to
overwrite files you changed locally – it lists them instead. `--force` overwrites and writes a backup to
`.kataster/backup/`.

## Design notes

- **`.claude/` is the source of truth.** OpenCode and Claude Code share skills, agents and hooks; `.opencode/` is an
  adapter, not a second workflow.
- **Plain Node, no build step.** Hooks and validators run on Node 22.18+ with one runtime dependency (`yaml`).
- **Generated files stay generated.** `BACKLOG.md` and `event-storming.md` are rendered; edit the sources.
- **The backlog is local by default.** One Markdown file per story; no issue tracker required. GitHub Issues and Jira
  are opt-in, and `docs/stories/` stays the mirror that validation and traceability run on.

was removed when the package was extracted – the examples are neutral, the stack is detected, and the language is

# Architecture decisions

`NNNN-slug.md`, sequential, never reused. Format and when to write one:
`.claude/skills/architect/ADR-FORMAT.md`.

# Prototypes

Throwaway code that answers one design question. The method is `.claude/skills/prototype/SKILL.md`.

- A prototype lives in `docs/prototypes/<slug>/` on a throwaway branch `prototype/<slug>`; it is never merged.
- The default branch keeps this README only. The prototype itself is a primary source on its branch.
- The decision it settled goes into the story (`Prototype: prototype/<slug> – <question> – <verdict>` in
  `## Context`) and, when it is a recurring rule, into `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md` as a G-number.
- One question, one self-contained HTML file, one timebox. No tests, no persistence, no production code.

# Stories

One Markdown file per story: `ST-NNN-short-title.md`. `BACKLOG.md` is generated – never edit it by hand.
Rules, format and splitting: `.claude/skills/user-stories/SKILL.md`.
Template: `.claude/skills/user-stories/templates/story-template.md`.

Workflow: `draft → review → ready-for-human-review → ready → in-progress → done` (plus `superseded`).

- The **spec linter** is the gate: `node .claude/skills/user-stories/scripts/lint-story.ts <file>` (or
  `kataster lint-story`). It checks frontmatter, `aggregate`/`command`/events against `docs/domain/events.yaml`,
  Gherkin `Given/When/Then` and the scenario limit – deterministically, no LLM.
- Green → `ready-for-human-review`; **the user approves `ready`**. `/implement` only picks up `ready`.
- **1-command rule:** one `type: domain` story = one command + its events on one aggregate, at most 4 scenarios.
- **Fast lane:** `type: chore` or `type: task` for UI tweaks, refactorings, dependencies and setup – no Gherkin
  matching, no formal reviews. `type: tech-task` keeps its checklist; `type: spike` is a timeboxed question.
- `ui: true` marks a story with a frontend part; it triggers the on-demand UX utility, never a gate.
- A story that turns out wrong goes back to `review` with an `[OPEN]` and a row in `OPEN_QUESTIONS.md`.
- `done` is final: a change to finished behaviour is a new story.

## Backlog backend

`docs/stories/` is the backlog when `.claude/project.json` has `backlog.provider: "local"` (the default). With
`"github"` or `"jira"`, the tracker is the source of truth and this directory is its **local mirror**:

- a story keeps its stable `ST-NNN` id and carries `external: { provider, key, url }`
- pull before reviewing or implementing, push after creating, changing or approving a story
- a story must be linked before it reaches `ready`
- the tracker wins on conflict; the local copy is backed up, never silently lost
- reviews and `OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` stay local; `BACKLOG.md` is generated from the mirror

Sync with `/backlog-sync`; the rules are in `.claude/skills/backlog/SKILL.md`.

Start with `/bootstrap` (greenfield) or `/adopt` (brownfield), then `/feature` for new work.

# Initiatives

Proposals for ideas larger than one feature, written by `/shape`. An initiative is **not** a work item: it has no
`ready`/`done`, creates no stories and never replaces `docs/stories/`. It answers four questions and ends with a
recommendation:

1. Should we do this at all?
2. Where does it belong – an existing bounded context, a new one, a shared library?
3. What changes, and what is genuinely new?
4. What does it roughly cost – in scope, range and risk?

File: `<slug>.md`, one per initiative. Status is `proposed` until the user accepts it; `parked` and `rejected` are
final until a new initiative replaces them. On handoff to `/feature`, set `promoted: <slug>` and let the stories
carry the label `feature:<slug>`.

```markdown
---
status: proposed          # proposed | accepted | parked | rejected
created: YYYY-MM-DD
source: ""                # optional ticket reference
promoted: ""              # feature:<slug> once slices are handed to /feature
---

# Initiative: <title>

## Problem & outcome
## Fit with the vision
## Placement
| Capability | Context | New/existing | Why | Confidence |
## Impact – change vs. build new
| Dimension | Change | New | Evidence |
## Slices
1. …
## Rough cost
| Currency | Estimate | Confidence | Basis |
## Risks & open questions
## Recommendation
```

Cost is always a range with a basis and a confidence – never a single number. An unknown is a line in the brief,
not a silent percentage.

# Brownfield: adopting an existing repository

The repository already works. The goal is not a rewrite and not a documentation exercise – it is to recover the
domain the code encodes, in the user's language, and then decide what to build next.

```bash
npx kataster init --brownfield
# in the harness
/adopt                      # map the repository, then choose a slice
/adopt apps/billing         # adopt one package
/adopt libs/shared-kernel   # adopt a shared library
```

## Adopt in slices, not in one pass

A monorepo with eighty packages cannot be understood in one session. `/adopt` therefore works in two levels:

1. **Repository map** – deterministic, no questions: which build tool drives the repository, where the packages
   are, how they depend on each other, which ones change most.
2. **One slice** – one domain plus at most one shared library. Deep evidence, grilling, package docs, checks.
   Then the next slice in a later session.

The map is generated from manifests and git history:

- `docs/architecture/repo-map.json` – packages, paths, kinds, internal dependencies, consumers, adoption ranking
- `docs/architecture/repo-map.md` – the same as a readable map, plus dependency edges and a suggested first slice
- the **repository block in `AGENTS.md`** – tooling, layout, commands, adopted slices
- `.claude/project.json` → `repo.tooling` – Nx, Turborepo, Bazel, pnpm/npm/yarn workspaces, Go, Cargo, Gradle, Maven

The map is facts, not domain. It says where code lives, never what a word means.

## What `/adopt` does

### 1. Chooses the slice with you

The ranking weighs recent churn, fan-in and kind – not size. The suggested slice is usually one domain plus the
shared library it uses most. You can pick another; the rule stays: **one domain, at most one shared library**.

A simple repository without monorepo tooling is one slice – then the whole repository is in scope.

### 2. Reads before it analyses

`CONTEXT.md`, `docs/`, `README*`, `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`, existing ADRs. Existing documentation is **primary
evidence** and outranks inference from code. Contradictions between docs and code are findings.

### 3. Dispatches read-only analysts for the slice

A monorepo gets three lenses:

| Lens | Typical evidence |
|---|---|
| Structure, data and entry points | manifests, entry points, schema, migrations, enums, external services, jobs, the slice's dependencies and consumers |
| Language, behaviour and tests | types, routes, UI texts, errors, validations, permissions, tests as executable specifications |
| Architecture, dependencies and history | layering and import direction from the repo map, build tooling, config that encodes a decision, `git log` hotspots |

A small repository without monorepo tooling gets the five classic lenses: structure and stack, domain language,
data and integrations, behaviour and tests, history and decisions.

Each analyst returns facts with `path:line`, candidate vocabulary, candidate events/commands/read models,
contradictions, and questions with a recommended answer. Confidence is `high`, `medium` or `low`.

### 4. Drafts the slice

- `CONTEXT.md` – the slice's terms, competing spellings under `_Avoid_`
- `docs/domain/events.yaml` – 10–25 candidate events, commands, actors, read models, flows, hotspots
- `docs/domain/context-map.md`, `docs/architecture/data-model.md` (as-is)
- `docs/engineering/conventions.md` – how the code actually works today, including the monorepo tooling
- `docs/adr/` – de-facto decisions worth recording (`status: proposed`)
- **package docs** – `<package>/AGENTS.md` plus `<package>/CLAUDE.md`, written by
  `node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/package-doc.ts <path>`

Everything uncertain is marked. The draft is a proposal, not a verdict.

### 5. Grills you against the draft

This is the core. Rounds of numbered questions on the frontier, each with a recommended answer:

> **Q1 – One concept, three names.** You call it `Order`, `Purchase` and `Checkout` in three places
> (`src/orders/*`, `src/api/checkout.ts`, `messages/en.json`). Is it one concept, and which is the domain word?
>
> ➡️ One concept, "Order"; `Checkout` is the UI action, `Purchase` should be avoided.

Answers update `CONTEXT.md`, `events.yaml` and the package's `AGENTS.md` immediately. Resolved hotspots get a
resolution; new uncertainty becomes a new hotspot.

### 6. Builds the safety net

For every confirmed hard rule, choose the cheapest deterministic enforcement: type system, lint/boundary check,
architecture or characterization test, hook, or documentation only. Brownfield checks start **report-only** with a
baseline of existing violations; only new violations fail. A hook that is red on day one gets switched off.

`/adopt` may add characterization tests and tooling. It never changes production code, and it never writes a test
that fails on existing behaviour – that would be a story.

### 7. Records the gap – stories only on request

| Class | Default |
|---|---|
| Exists and is intended | Documentation (data model, context map) – no action |
| Exists but contradicts the model | Candidate in the gap register |
| Missing | Candidate in the gap register |
| Dead | Candidate: removal or an explicit "leave it" |

**The first adoption pass creates no stories.** It records the gap in `docs/domain/adoption-report.md` (and open
questions in `OPEN_QUESTIONS.md`), so the model can be reviewed before anyone commits to work. Only
`/adopt <scope> --stories` (or an explicit "turn these into stories") turns the selected gaps into stories in the
main session (spec engineer, spec linter gate).

**Behaviour that already works does not become a story.** That turns the backlog into a description of the past.

### 8. Writes the report and marks the slice adopted

`docs/domain/adoption-report.md`: scope, map and slice, facts, confirmed model, package docs, contradictions, rules
and checks, gaps, what was deliberately left alone, open hotspots, next slice.

```bash
node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/repo-map.ts --adopt apps/billing
```

The next session sees the progress in `AGENTS.md` and the map, and starts the next slice with
`/adopt <path>`.

## What lives where

| File | Loaded | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` (root) | every session | repository structure, commands, hard conventions, links – **no domain** |
| `<package>/AGENTS.md` | when working in that package | purpose, key entities or public API, interfaces, pitfalls, boundaries |
| `<package>/CLAUDE.md` | same, for Claude Code | one line: `@AGENTS.md` |
| `<group>/AGENTS.md` | when working under that group | rules for a whole group, e.g. `libs/**` – plus `<group>/CLAUDE.md` |
| `.claude/rules/*.md` | when a matching file is touched (both harnesses) | path-scoped rules for patterns a directory cannot express |
| `docs/architecture/boundaries.yaml` | on demand / on check | allowed and forbidden dependency edges (first match wins) |
| `docs/architecture/boundaries.baseline.json` | on check | existing violations, so only new ones fail |
| `docs/engineering/checks.yaml` | on check | what runs at edit time and at Stop/CI |
| `docs/architecture/repo-map.md` | on demand | generated map: packages, edges, consumers, ranking |
| `CONTEXT.md` | every session | the domain language |

Nested `AGENTS.md` is loaded on demand by OpenCode; Claude Code loads the nested `CLAUDE.md` when it reads or
edits a file there. That is why every package gets both files.

## Monorepos and shared libraries

The detected tool is used, not re-implemented:

| Tool | One package | Affected only |
|---|---|---|
| Nx | `nx run <project>:test` | `nx affected -t test` |
| Turborepo | `turbo run test --filter=<package>` | `turbo run test --filter='...[HEAD^1]'` |
| Bazel | `bazel test //<package>/...` | – (query at work time) |
| pnpm | `pnpm --filter <package> test` | `pnpm -r --filter '...[HEAD^1]' test` |
| npm/yarn workspaces | `npm run test --workspace <package>` / `yarn workspace <package> test` | – |
| Go / Cargo / Gradle / Maven | language-specific, in the package doc | – |

When a shared library changes, its consumers from the map are the first thing to check; run their tests or the
affected set. The library's `AGENTS.md` records its public API, consumers and compatibility rules.

The map asks the build tool for its own graph and stores it as an optional `toolGraph` next to the manifest
graph – Turborepo via `turbo run <task> --dry=json`, Nx via `nx graph --file=<temp>`, Bazel from the `deps`
attributes in `BUILD`/`BUILD.bazel`. The fast loop then uses it:

```bash
# which packages are affected by these files, including shared-library dependents?
node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/affected.ts --changed libs/shared-kernel/src/index.ts

# or against a base ref; the tool's native affected filter is emitted
node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/affected.ts --base origin/main

# execute the printed command
node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/affected.ts --changed apps/billing/src/index.ts --run
```

The output is a native command: Turborepo gets `turbo run test --filter=…`, Nx `nx run-many -p …` or
`nx affected`, Bazel `bazel test //pkg/...`, and so on. Nx project names are resolved from the graph, so
`billing` and `@acme/billing` do not have to match. If the tool is not installed (or does not answer), the
manifest graph is used instead – the workflow never depends on the tool being present.

## Rules, boundaries and checks

Confirmed architecture rules become deterministic, not prose:

```bash
node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/boundary-check.ts --init
# edit docs/architecture/boundaries.yaml with the rules the user confirmed
node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/boundary-check.ts --update-baseline
node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/boundary-check.ts
```

`boundaries.yaml` holds edges, not stories:

```yaml
version: 1
engine: auto          # scan JS/TS imports, or command for your own tool
command: ""
rules:
  - id: shared-libs-are-leaves
    from: "libs/**"
    to: ["apps/**", "services/**"]
    effect: deny
    reason: "Shared libraries never import applications or services."
```

Rules are evaluated in order; the first matching `from` → `to` pair decides, no match means allow. The `scan`
engine reads JS/TS imports; `command` runs dependency-cruiser, Nx module boundaries, Bazel, ArchUnit,
import-linter or your own script and ratchets its failure output.

**Baseline/ratchet:** `--update-baseline` freezes what already exists. After that only new violations fail, so a
brownfield repository is green on day one and the baseline shrinks over time. The checks are wired once through
`project-check.ts`; `docs/engineering/checks.yaml` decides which check runs at edit time (changed file only) and
which at Stop/CI.

Path-scoped rules that a directory cannot express get a file with `paths:`:

```bash
node .claude/skills/adopt/scripts/rule-doc.ts libs-shared --paths "libs/**" --title "Shared libraries"
```

A rule for a whole directory belongs in `<dir>/AGENTS.md` (plus its one-line `CLAUDE.md`) – that is the mechanism
both harnesses load on demand. Path-scoped rules are read natively by Claude Code; in OpenCode the plugin attaches
the matching rule as session context as soon as a file under its globs is read or written.

## Rules that make adoption work

- **Adopt in slices.** One bounded context completely beats the whole repository shallowly.
- **Code names are evidence, not language.** `OrderService.place()` suggests "Order placed"; the user decides.
- **Never change production code.** The output is language, model, decisions, docs and checks.
- **An 80% confirmed model with 20% hotspots beats a 100% invented one.**
- **The user owns the language.** Propose a better word; don't rename the domain alone.
- **The root `AGENTS.md` stays free of domain.** Structure and commands only.

## After adoption

```bash
git diff                    # only CONTEXT.md, docs/, package docs and tooling changed
/adopt <next>               # next slice
/adopt <scope> --stories    # turn the selected gaps into stories, when you want a backlog
/feature <idea | ticket>    # next work, now that the domain has a language
/shape <large idea>         # new service/context/migration: placement, impact, slices, cost range
/implement                  # once a story is ready
```

With a tracker (`backlog.provider` = `github` or `jira`), pull before adopting or reviewing and push the derived
stories afterwards. The tracker is the source of truth; `docs/stories/` is the mirror.

# Concepts

The vocabulary the workflow uses, and why each piece exists.

## Grilling

An interview in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are settled – the questions that
can be asked now without guessing at answers you haven't heard. Each question is numbered and carries a recommended
answer, worded so that "yes" accepts it. Answers reshape the tree and push the frontier outward.

Two rules make it work:

- **Facts are the agent's job, decisions are the user's.** Files, code, docs, history – look it up. Never ask the
  user something you could find yourself.
- **Do not act until the frontier is empty** and the user confirms a shared understanding.

`/grill-me` is the pure form. `/grill-with-docs` adds the glossary and ADRs. Every discovery command embeds it.

## The artifacts

| Artifact | What it is | Who owns it |
|---|---|---|
| `CONTEXT.md` | Glossary – the ubiquitous language. One canonical word per concept, alternatives under `_Avoid_` | user, maintained by the agent |
| `docs/domain/events.yaml` | Event storming model: actors, contexts, aggregates, events, commands, policies, read models, hotspots, flows | user, written by the agent |
| `docs/domain/context-map.md` | Bounded contexts and their relationships (DDD patterns) | domain-architect |
| `docs/architecture/data-model.md` | Logical, stack-neutral model per aggregate; lifecycle and ER diagrams | domain-architect |
| `docs/engineering/conventions.md` | How code is built here, including the seam catalog | user |
| `docs/adr/` | Architecture decisions. `proposed` until the user accepts; accepted ones are superseded, never edited | user |
| `docs/stories/` | The backlog. One Markdown file per story; `BACKLOG.md` is generated. With a tracker, this is the local mirror | main session as spec engineer; spec linter; `/backlog-sync` with a tracker |
| `docs/product/vision.md` | Problem, user groups, goals, non-goals, success criteria | user |
| `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md` | The interface yardstick, as numbered rules with date and reason | ux-designer, approved by user |
| `docs/prototypes/<slug>/` | Throwaway prototypes on their own branch; only the README stays on the default branch | ux-designer; verdict in the story and the guidelines |

## Events, commands, aggregates

- An **event** is a business fact in the past tense: "Order placed". Not a button click, not "Record saved".
- A **command** is an intent that produces events: "Place order". It has an actor (or a policy) and rules.
- A **policy** is "whenever <event>, then <command>" – including time-triggered ones.
- A **read model** is what an actor needs to decide to send a command.
- An **aggregate** protects the invariants that must be consistent *immediately*. Everything else is eventually
  consistent via events and policies.
- An **invariant** is stated once, on the aggregate. A command's rules list only what it adds beyond them.

IDs are prefixed and stable: `ACT-`, `EXT-`, `BC-`, `AGG-`, `EVT-`, `CMD-`, `POL-`, `RM-`, `HS-`, `FLOW-`, `ST-`.
The code carries the same IDs, which is what makes traceability checkable.

## Stories

A story is a vertical slice of observable behaviour: `draft → review → ready-for-human-review → ready →
in-progress → done` (plus `superseded`).

- **The linter is the gate.** `lint-story.ts` checks the spec deterministically. Green → `ready-for-human-review`;
  the user approves `ready`.
- **Discovery ends at `ready`.** Engineering moves `ready → in-progress → done`.
- **1-command rule.** One domain story = one command + its events on one aggregate, at most 4 scenarios. A second
  command is a second story.
- **Fast lane.** `type: chore`/`task` for UI tweaks, refactors, dependencies and setup – no Gherkin matching, no
  formal reviews.
- **A story that turns out wrong goes back to `review`** with an `[OPEN]` and a row in `OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` – never
  guessed into shape during implementation.
- **`done` is final.** A change to finished behaviour is a new story.
- **A scenario title becomes a test title**: `ST-NNN: <scenario title>`. `verify.ts` checks the link for domain
  stories.

### Stories from tickets

`/feature` can start from an `ST-NNN`, a GitHub issue (`#123` or URL), a Jira key or a pasted ticket. The ticket is
**evidence, not a specification**: its acceptance criteria are grilled like any other claim, contradictions with the
model are findings, and the source is recorded in the story (`Source: …`). A bug gets one regression story with the
label `bug`; if the documented rule itself is wrong, it is a feature, because the rule changes. The intake is
read-only – it never writes stories, `external` links or sync state.

## Initiatives

An **initiative** is a proposal for an idea larger than one feature: a new service, a new bounded context, a
migration, a cross-context capability. `/shape` writes it to `docs/product/initiatives/<slug>.md` after the user
confirms the summary. It answers four questions: should we, where does it belong, what changes vs. what is new, and
what does it roughly cost. It ends with one recommendation: go, go with slice 1, spike first, needs discovery, park
or no-go.

An initiative is **not** a work item: no `ready`/`done`, no stories, no second backlog. The cost is always a range
with a basis and a confidence – an analogue service is evidence, not a template. Each accepted slice then goes
through `/feature`, which creates the stories and runs the review.

## Prototypes

A **prototype** is throwaway code that answers one design question. It is not a first draft: no tests, no
persistence, no production path. The question decides the branch – `ui` (what should it look like) or `logic`
(does the state model feel right). In discovery it is one self-contained HTML file under
`docs/prototypes/<slug>/`, built by the `ux-designer`; a question that needs the real application page is built
by the main session during `/implement`.

`/feature --prototype` (or a proposal from the UX frontier during grilling) adds the phase between grilling and
the stories. The verdict goes into the story (`Prototype: prototype/<slug> – <question> – <verdict>`) and, when
it is a recurring rule, into `ux-guidelines.md` as a G-number. The code is captured on a throwaway branch
`prototype/<slug>` and never merged. `/implement --prototype` does the same for an open UI question during
engineering; if it changes the story, the story goes back to `review`.

## The seam catalog

A **seam** is where a test attaches. Testing everything everywhere is not affordable, so the project agrees up front
which kind of code is tested at which seam – pure rule, command, read model, page. That catalog lives in
`docs/engineering/conventions.md`. `/implement` only stops for the user when a story needs a seam that is not in it.

## Review lanes

Review effort follows the risk of the diff, not a fixed checklist:

- **Light lane** – small, no domain events, no command, no migration, no input handling, no new dependency:
  acceptance tester only.
- **Normal lane** – code reviewer and acceptance tester in parallel, plus a bug-focused or security-focused pass when
  the diff touches shared platform code or input/auth/uploads.

## The acceptance verdict

The **acceptance tester decides** whether a story is done, not the user. The user reviews the pull request and
merges. That keeps one checkpoint with the user (merge) instead of two.

## Why a local mirror

One Markdown file per story, versioned with the code, validated by a hook, rendered into `BACKLOG.md`. The agent can
read and write it deterministically, and the domain model and the stories can be checked against each other.

That is the whole answer for `backlog.provider: "local"`. Teams that already work in a tracker get the same properties
with `"github"` or `"jira"`: the tracker is the source of truth, `docs/stories/` is a synchronized mirror, and the
mirror is what validation, test traceability and offline work run on. The story keeps its `ST-NNN` id; the tracker key
lives in `external`. Only the backlog core syncs – reviews and open questions stay local. The tracker wins a conflict;
the local file is backed up before it is overwritten.

GitHub syncs through `gh`; Jira through `mcp-atlassian`, because MCP is reachable only from the agent.

# Greenfield: starting a new project

```bash
npx kataster init --greenfield
# in the harness
/bootstrap
```

The order is fixed: **vision → domain → architecture → UX → stories**. Technology comes after the domain, never
before it.

For an idea that is larger than one project – several services, a new product line – `/shape` can frame it first.
Without a domain model it will stop at `unknown` placement and send you back here; that is the correct answer, not
a failure.

## Phase 1 – Vision

The frontier is every `[OPEN]` in `docs/product/vision.md`: problem, user groups, goals, non-goals, success criteria,
constraints, the domain in one paragraph. Grilled in rounds, each question with a recommended answer.

Two rules that do the most work:

- **No technology in this phase.** If the user starts with a framework, park it: that is an ADR after the domain,
  and the domain may change the answer.
- **Force a non-goal.** A vision without a "we will not do this" is a wish list.

## Phase 2 – Event storming

Big-picture storming, phases 1–6 of the `event-storming` skill:

1. 8–15 suspected events, in the user's words, past tense
2. Timeline into flows, pivotal events marked
3. Hotspots, grilled where the user can decide now
4. Commands and actors
5. Policies, including time-triggered ones
6. Read models

`docs/domain/events.yaml` is written after every phase and validated by a hook.

## Phase 3 – Domain model and architecture

`domain-architect` proposes bounded contexts, the context map, aggregates with testable invariants, and the
logical data model. Then, in this order:

1. **Shape** – the simplest architecture that meets the documented requirements. A monolith is the default;
   anything distributed cites a requirement.
2. **Tech stack** – one ADR, `status: proposed`, driving requirements cited. Only the user sets `accepted`.
3. **Other decisions** – only the ones that pass the architect's three criteria.

## Phase 4 – UX yardstick

Devices and design size, UI language(s), the states every screen needs (empty, full, rejected, no permission), and
the recurring patterns worth a guideline number. Written as rules into `docs/product/ux-guidelines.md`, with date
and reason.

## Phase 5 – Foundation stories and the first slice

Two kinds of work, kept apart:

- **Foundation tech tasks** – repository skeleton, one quality command (`verify`), CI, test harness, auth/roles if
  the vision needs them, deployment. Minimal, with `depends_on`, just in time.
- **The first vertical slice** – the smallest set of stories that delivers one real end-to-end path from the
  vision, each with Gherkin scenarios.

One story = one command on one aggregate, at most 4 scenarios; no implementation plan inside a domain story; every domain story links `aggregate`, `command` and its `events`.

## Phase 6 – Review

`/review-stories` – the spec linter checks frontmatter, aggregate/command/events, Gherkin and the scenario limit.
Green → `ready-for-human-review`; you approve every `ready`. With a tracker, pull before the review and push the
approved stories afterwards (`/backlog-sync`).

## Phase 7 – Build

```bash
node .claude/skills/implement/scripts/verify.ts   # should be green
/implement                                        # first foundation story
```

Then `/feature <idea | ticket>` for everything after that, `/groom-backlog` once the first bounded context is complete.

## Checkpoints

After vision, after storming, after the model, after the stories – summarize in 3–5 lines and ask whether to
continue. A bootstrap that runs to the end without a checkpoint produces a beautiful model nobody agreed to.

# Install, upgrade, troubleshoot

## Install

```bash
npx kataster init [dir]
```

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--brownfield` / `--greenfield` | Sets the starting path (default: detected from the code) |
| `--name <name>` | Project name (default: `package.json` name, else directory name) |
| `--ui-language <lang>` | Language of the user interface (default `en`) |
| `--artifacts <lang>` | Language of docs, stories, code comments (default `en`) |
| `--backlog <provider>` | Where stories live: `local` (default), `github`, `jira` |
| `--jira-project <key>` | Jira project key (with `--backlog jira`) |
| `--github-repo <repo>` | `owner/name` for a GitHub backlog (default: the current repository) |
| `--yes`, `-y` | Non-interactive: accept the detected defaults |
| `--no-install` | Skip `npm install --prefix .claude` |
| `--dry-run` | Show what would happen, write nothing |

The installer:

- copies `.claude/`, `.opencode/`, `AGENTS.md` and the `docs/` skeleton,
- **merges** into an existing `AGENTS.md` (marker block), `.claude/settings.json` (hooks and permissions) and
  `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` (watcher ignore list),
- detects stack, package manager, code roots and commands into `.claude/project.json`,
- records the backlog backend in `.claude/project.json` (`local`, `github` or `jira`),
- adds `.claude/node_modules/`, `.claude/state/` and `.kataster/` to `.gitignore`,
- installs the tooling dependency (`yaml`) into `.claude/`,
- records every managed file with a hash in `.claude/install.json`.

Existing `CONTEXT.md` and `docs/` are never overwritten.

## Verify the installation

```bash
npx kataster doctor
```

Checks Node version, workflow files, manifest, profile, tooling dependencies, the docs skeleton, whether
`docs/domain/events.yaml` validates, and the backlog backend (Jira project/MCP server or GitHub CLI/auth).

## Upgrade

```bash
npx kataster upgrade
```

- Workflow files that you did not change are replaced.
- Workflow files you **did** change are kept and listed as conflicts; `--force` overwrites them and writes a backup
  to `.kataster/backup/<timestamp>/`.
- Project content (`CONTEXT.md`, `docs/`, `.claude/project.json`) is never touched.
- An installation made under the old name (La Guardia) is migrated in place: `.laguardia/` becomes `.kataster/`, the
  OpenCode adapter moves to `.opencode/plugins/kataster/`, and the marker blocks in `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` are
  rewritten. `backlog.labelPrefix` in `project.json` is kept, so labels already in GitHub or Jira stay valid.
- An existing `project.json` keeps its content. If it predates the backlog backend, add the `backlog` section by hand
  (see the README) – without it the provider stays `local`.
- An extra installed by an older version (`--with shadcn`, up to 0.2.1) stays on disk as a project file; upgrade no
  longer touches it. Delete `.claude/skills/shadcn/` if you do not want it.

## Harness setup

### OpenCode

Nothing to configure. `.opencode/commands/` provides the slash commands, `.opencode/agents/` the subagents, and
`.opencode/plugins/kataster/index.ts` wires the `.claude/hooks/*.ts` scripts into OpenCode's hook events.
`.opencode/opencode.jsonc` only holds watcher ignores.

### Claude Code

`.claude/settings.json` wires the same hooks (`SessionStart`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`). Skills in
`.claude/skills/` and agents in `.claude/agents/` are discovered automatically. Approve the project hooks once when
Claude Code asks.

### Both

Both harnesses read `AGENTS.md`. Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` first; the installer creates one containing
`@AGENTS.md`, or adds that import block to an existing `CLAUDE.md` without touching your house rules. The workflow
lives in `.claude/`; `.opencode/` is an adapter. An existing `.claude/` is merged: skills, rules and settings that
do not collide with a workflow file are left alone.

`local` needs nothing. `github` needs the `gh` CLI, authenticated with the `repo` scope; set
`backlog.github.repo` if it is not the current repository. `jira` needs the `mcp-atlassian` server in your harness and
a real `backlog.jira.project`; the status and priority maps must match the project's workflow.

- Claude Code: add the server to `.mcp.json` and approve it once.
- OpenCode: add it to the `mcp` block in `opencode.jsonc`.

{

    "mcp-atlassian": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["uvx", "mcp-atlassian"],
      "enabled": true,
      "environment": { "JIRA_URL": "https://…", "JIRA_USERNAME": "…", "JIRA_API_TOKEN": "…" }

## Troubleshooting

**"Tooling dependencies are missing"** – run `npm install --prefix .claude`. The validators and hooks need `yaml`.

**Hooks don't run in OpenCode** – the plugin spawns the project's `node`. If Node is not on `PATH`, set
`KATASTER_NODE` to the binary.

**`verify` skips project checks** – `commands` in `.claude/project.json` are empty. Fill in `lint`, `typecheck`,
`test` (and `e2e`) with the commands this repository actually uses.

**The stack detection is wrong** – it is a starting point. Edit `.claude/project.json`; nothing else reads the
detection.

**The backlog sync fails** – `npx kataster doctor` checks the provider. GitHub: `gh auth status`. Jira: the
`mcp-atlassian` server must be configured in the harness and `backlog.jira.project` must be set.
`node .claude/skills/backlog/scripts/backlog-status.ts` shows what is linked and what drifted.

**An accepted ADR can't be edited** – by design. Write a new ADR and set the old one's status to
`superseded by ADR-NNNN`. The hook allows exactly that.

**Upgrade reports conflicts** – those are files you changed. Review the diff, then either keep your version or run
`upgrade --force` (a backup is written to `.kataster/backup/`).
`upgrade --force` (backup is written).

# Release

## 1. Prepare

1. Bump `version` in `package.json`. The package is `0.x`: a breaking change – a renamed command, a removed flag, a
   moved directory – bumps the minor number, everything else the patch number.
2. Move the `Unreleased` section of `CHANGELOG.md` under the new version.
3. Check the tree:

```bash
npm install --prefix .claude --no-audit --no-fund
npm run typecheck --prefix .claude
npm test
npm pack --dry-run        # 148 files, 218 kB – no examples/, no node_modules, no state/
```

4. Install the tarball once and start a throwaway project with it – a tarball that installs is not the same as a
   tarball that works:

```bash
npm pack
npm install -g --prefix "$(mktemp -d)" ./kataster-*.tgz
kataster init /tmp/smoke --yes
kataster doctor /tmp/smoke
```

## 2. Publish

### Through CI (the normal case)

The tag publishes. `v0.2.0` starts `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which checks that the tag matches
`package.json`, runs the type check and the suite, then publishes over OIDC – no npm token in the repository, no
one-time password, and provenance attestations are written automatically.

```bash
git push origin main
git tag -a v0.2.0 -m "Kataster 0.2.0"
git push origin v0.2.0
gh run watch
```

If the tag and `package.json` disagree, the workflow fails before it publishes – bump the version first, then tag.

### The first time only: trusted publisher

npm has to know which workflow may publish. On npmjs.com → `kataster` → Settings → **Trusted publishing** →
GitHub Actions:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Organization or user | `hemi1986` |
| Repository | `kataster` |
| Workflow filename | `release.yml` |
| Environment name | – (leave empty) |
| Allowed actions | **Allow npm publish** (the default `npm stage publish` alone is not enough) |

The first publish has to succeed within **two days**, otherwise the configuration expires and has to be created
again. Once it works, lock the old path down: Settings → **Publishing access** → "Require two-factor authentication
and disallow tokens". Trusted publishers keep working; tokens and OTP stop working.

### By hand (fallback)

If CI is unavailable or a version has to go out without a tag:

```bash
npm login                 # once per machine
npm publish --access public
```

`prepublishOnly` runs the test suite, so a red suite cannot be published.

## 3. Verify

```bash
npm view kataster version
npx kataster@latest --version
```

The package page shows a provenance badge (`built and signed on GitHub Actions`) and the workflow run is linked to
the tag. A missing badge means the publish did not go through trusted publishing. The registry can take a minute or
two before a new version appears; `npm view kataster version` is the source of truth, not the cache in `npx`.

## What ships

`package.json` → `files` decides:

- `bin/`, `src/` – the CLI and installer
- `.claude/`, `.opencode/` – the payload the installer copies
- `templates/` – docs skeleton
- `guide/`, `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `LICENSE`

Not shipped: `test/`, `examples/`, `.github/`. `examples/` contains project-specific facts and is reference material
for the repository only.

5. **Test quality** (tdd skill) – tests sit at the agreed seams and go through public interfaces; flag implementation-coupled tests (mocked internal collaborators, database queried to verify a command), tautological assertions (expected value computed like the code does), and scenarios whose test does not actually check the scenario's "Then".
6. **Design** (codebase-design skill) – shallow modules, pass-throughs, seams with one adapter, leaking modules. Name the deepening; don't design it.
7. **Code smells** – judgement calls, a documented convention always wins: Mysterious Name, Duplicated Code, Feature Envy, Data Clumps, Primitive Obsession (e.g. a domain identifier as a bare string), Repeated Switches, Shotgun Surgery, Divergent Change, Speculative Generality (anything the story doesn't ask for), Message Chains, Middle Man, Refused Bequest.
